pests.name: Brown planthopper
pests.hint: Hopperburn: round patches of plants that dry and turn brown, with insects at the base.

rice: Stops the hoppers feeding at once, but they take two to four days to die, so do not spray again too soon.
Same group 4A as imidacloprid, which this hopper resists, and some trials saw hoppers rebound after it. Toxic to bees.
Kills nymphs only, not adults, and works slowly. Resisted in parts of Asia, so use it once a crop.
Only the thiamethoxam acts on hoppers. Worth it when stem borers need control at the same time.
Same group 4A as imidacloprid, which this hopper resists. Toxic to bees. Switch groups after one spray.
Weak on planthoppers. Keep it for stem borers and whorl maggot.
Very toxic to fish, shrimp and bees and harsh on spiders, and resistance is rising in Asia. A last resort.
Highly toxic to people, fish, ducks and birds, and linked to hopper resurgence. A last resort only.
Kills the spiders and mirid bugs that eat hoppers. One spray at most, late in the crop.
Kills the spiders and mirid bugs that eat hoppers. One spray at most, late in the crop.
Very toxic to fish, ducks and birds, and harsh on the hoppers' enemies. A last resort.
The isoprocarb half is of the same family as BPMC, which this hopper resists here. The buprofezin half works on nymphs only.
Imidacloprid no longer controls this hopper well, and fipronil is very toxic to fish and shrimp.
Same family as BPMC, which planthoppers here resist strongly. Expect weak results.

avoid: Diazinon
Known in trials to make brown planthopper come back worse after spraying.
Fenobucarb (BPMC) plus chlorpyrifos
Hoppers here resist BPMC, and chlorpyrifos kills their enemies, so outbreaks can follow.
Acephate
Trials in South Asia saw brown planthopper come back in bigger numbers after acephate sprays.
Cypermethrin
Pyrethroids kill the spiders and bugs that eat hoppers, and planthoppers come back worse after the spray.
Alpha cypermethrin
Pyrethroids kill the spiders and bugs that eat hoppers, and planthoppers come back worse after the spray.
Chlorpyrifos
Field trials saw hoppers rise and their predators fall after chlorpyrifos sprays, ending above unsprayed rice.
Lambda cyhalothrin plus thiamethoxam
The pyrethroid in it kills spiders and lets planthoppers come back worse.
Chlorpyrifos plus cypermethrin
The pyrethroid and the organophosphate kill the hoppers' enemies, and planthoppers come back worse.
Beta cypermethrin
Pyrethroids kill the spiders and bugs that eat hoppers, and planthoppers come back worse after the spray.
Fenobucarb (BPMC)
Brown planthopper in the Philippines and much of Asia now resists BPMC strongly. It no longer pays.
Bifenthrin plus clothianidin
The pyrethroid in it kills spiders and lets planthoppers come back worse.
Phenthoate plus fenobucarb (BPMC)
Hoppers here resist BPMC, and the mix kills the spiders that hold them down.
Acephate plus imidacloprid
Imidacloprid no longer controls this hopper well, and acephate can bring it back in bigger numbers.
Esfenvalerate
Pyrethroids kill the spiders and bugs that eat hoppers, and planthoppers come back worse after the spray.
Permethrin
Pyrethroids kill the spiders and bugs that eat hoppers, and planthoppers come back worse after the spray.
prevent: Plant a resistant variety, and plant together with your neighbors with a fallow of one to two months between crops.
Space hills about 20 by 20 cm, split the nitrogen into three doses and keep potassium enough. Dense, lush rice breeds hoppers.
Use alternate wetting and drying from about 21 to 30 days after transplanting. Hoppers like a wet, humid base.
No insecticide in the first 30 to 40 days after transplanting. Early sprays kill the spiders that keep hoppers down.
Keep seedbeds away from lights, flood the seedbed for a day to drown hoppers, and plow under ratoons after harvest.
bio: Wolf spiders, mirid bugs (Cyrtorhinus), lady beetles and water striders eat hoppers and eggs. Count them before you spray.
The fungus Metarhizium anisopliae infects hoppers in humid weather.
Ducks let into the paddy once the plants are well rooted eat many hoppers.
pests.threshold: From 30 days after transplanting, tap 20 hills a week over the water and count hoppers and spiders. At 1 hopper per tiller or fewer, do nothing. Consider a spray only from booting on, when counts reach 25 or more per hill and hoppers outnumber spiders and mirid bugs.
pests.rotate: Brown planthopper in Asia resists imidacloprid and BPMC, and resistance to buprofezin, fipronil and thiamethoxam is rising. Use each group at most once a crop and switch among pymetrozine (9B), triflumezopyrim (4E), buprofezin (16) and dinotefuran (4A).

pests.name: Rice black bug
pests.hint: Dead hearts, whiteheads and bugburn patches. The bugs hide at the base of the hill by day.

rice: Systemic, so it reaches bugs hiding at the base of the hill. Toxic to bees. Gives only short relief alone.
Raise the water first so the bugs climb, then spray in the cool hours. Kills spiders and is very toxic to fish.
A pyrethroid known to set off planthopper outbreaks, and very toxic to fish. A last resort.
A pyrethroid: kills spiders and can make planthoppers flare. Very toxic to fish. A last resort.
A pyrethroid: kills spiders and can make planthoppers flare. Very toxic to fish. A last resort.
A pyrethroid: kills spiders and can make planthoppers flare. Very toxic to fish. A last resort.

avoid: Pymetrozine
Made for hoppers. It does little against stink bugs such as the black bug.
prevent: Plant varieties of the same maturity within a month of the barangay's usual date, over about 1 km around you.
Keep weeds down in the field and on the bunds, and apply nitrogen at the right rate in splits.
Raise the water to 8 to 10 cm for one to two days to stop eggs hatching, after checking the eggs for wasps.
Run bright light traps from two days before to three days after the full moon, and bury the catch.
Plow right after harvest and keep the stubble under water until it rots.
Tolerant varieties that replace lost tillers, and direct seeding with fewer tillers per hill, both help.
bio: The fungus Metarhizium anisopliae kills young and grown bugs. Where it is sold, spray it on the base of the hills.
The egg wasp Telenomus triptus lives inside black bug eggs. Crickets, spiders, ground beetles, lady beetles and red ants help too.
Ducks herded into insecticide free fields from a month after transplanting to heading eat many bugs.
pests.threshold: Pick 20 hills across the field and count eggs, nymphs and adults at the base. At 5 bugs per hill or fewer, no insecticide: flood and use Metarhizium. Above 5 per hill, a spray may pay, after raising the water so the bugs climb the leaves.

pests.name: Rice bug (atangya)
pests.hint: Empty or spotted grains at the milk stage, and a strong smell in the field.

rice: Fast on bugs, but very toxic to fish and kills spiders. Check for planthoppers first, since it can make them flare.
Breaks down within days, so it is one of the milder choices, but it is still toxic to fish and bees.
The pyrethroid half is very toxic to fish and kills spiders. Use it only when the count calls for it.
Systemic, so it reaches bugs feeding on the panicle. Toxic to bees, so spray late in the afternoon.
A pyrethroid: very toxic to fish and kills spiders. Check for planthoppers first, since it can make them flare.
Works well on the bugs but is very toxic to fish, ducks and birds. Keep ducks out and do not drain the water into fishponds.
Very toxic to fish, shrimp and bees, and stronger than a rice bug needs. Keep it as a last resort.
An old organophosphate known to bring planthoppers back worse. A last resort only.
Very toxic to bees. If you must use it, spray late in the day when no bees visit the flowering rice.
The pyrethroid most often linked to planthopper outbreaks, and very toxic to fish. A last resort for rice bug.
Very toxic to birds and fish. An old product kept only as a last resort.
Broad spectrum mix that kills the spiders and egg wasps working for you. A last resort only.
Kills spiders and fish and can flare planthoppers late in the crop. A last resort only.

prevent: Cut grassy weeds on the pilapil, the canals and the field edges before the crop flowers, so the bugs have nowhere to breed and wait.
Plant in the same weeks as your neighbors after a fallow of a month or more, so bugs cannot move from early fields to late ones.
Level the field and give even water and fertilizer, so the whole lot flowers and passes the milk stage together.
While numbers are low, sweep a net through the crop at dawn, or set baits of rotting snail or crab to gather the bugs, then destroy them.
Where you can, grow an awned variety. Awns, and panicles that stay longer in the leaf sheath, give some protection.
bio: Tiny egg wasps (Gryon) and long horned grasshoppers destroy rice bug eggs on the leaves.
Spiders, field crickets and lady beetles eat nymphs and adults. Skip broad sprays early in the crop so they build up.
The fungus Beauveria bassiana infects the bugs in wet, humid weather.
pests.threshold: From the start of flowering to hard dough, walk the field at dawn or late afternoon every few days and count bugs on 20 hills. Act only when you find more than 10 bugs in 20 hills, or more than 5 bugs per square meter at the milk stage.

pests.name: Rice leaffolder
pests.hint: Leaves folded into tubes with white streaks where the caterpillar scraped the green.

rice: Kind to spiders and wasps. Spray only to save the flag leaf, and do not use group 28 twice in a row.
Works on young caterpillars. Spray at the flag leaf stage only, never in the first 40 days.
Only the chlorantraniliprole acts on leaffolder. Pay for the mix only when hoppers need control too.
Same group 28 as chlorantraniliprole, so never use the two one after the other.
Makes caterpillars molt too early and die. Slow, but kind to spiders and wasps.
Kills caterpillars, but also the spiders and wasps that hold leaffolder and planthoppers down. Never early.
Kills caterpillars, but also the spiders and wasps that hold leaffolder and planthoppers down. Never early.
Highly toxic to people and harsh on natural enemies. A last resort only.
Very toxic to fish, shrimp and bees. Far more than a leaffolder needs. A last resort.
Kills spiders and wasps and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
A granule that does little for caterpillars in folded leaves, and it is highly toxic to people, fish and birds.
A neem product. Mild and short lived. It only slows young caterpillars.

avoid: Clothianidin
Made for sucking insects such as hoppers. It does little against caterpillars inside the fold.
prevent: Keep every insecticide off the crop for the first 30 to 40 days. Early leaf damage rarely costs grain.
Plant at a moderate density and give balanced fertilizer. Lush, dark green rice draws the moths.
Remove grassy weeds in the field and on the bunds, and cut back branches that shade the paddy edge.
Follow rice with another crop or a fallow, avoid ratooning, and flood and plow the field after harvest.
Use a resistant variety where your technician has one.
bio: Many small wasps lay their eggs in leaffolder eggs and caterpillars. Spiders and crickets eat the rest.
Flowering plants on the bunds feed the wasps with nectar and keep them in the field.
Where a Bt product for caterpillars is sold, it spares the wasps. Aim it at young caterpillars.
pests.threshold: Scout every week from tillering to flowering and open a few fresh folds. Before booting the crop regrows lost leaf, so do not spray. From booting on, act only when the flag leaf and the two leaves below it are heading toward more than half eaten and live caterpillars are in the folds.
pests.rotate: Leaffolder in China has grown less sensitive to chlorantraniliprole after heavy use. Do not spray group 28 twice in a row. Switch with cartap (14), indoxacarb (22A) or tebufenozide (18).

pests.name: Rice stem borer
pests.sci: Scirpophaga incertulas, Scirpophaga innotata, Chilo suppressalis
pests.hint: The central shoot dries up and pulls out easily, which is a deadheart.

rice: Hits young larvae best, soon after the eggs hatch and before they bore deep into the stem.
Spray when the eggs hatch, before larvae bore in. Kind to spiders and wasps. Do not use group 28 on two crops in a row.
The chlorantraniliprole does the borer work. Pay for the mix only when planthoppers need control too.
Same group 28 as chlorantraniliprole, so never use the two one after the other.
Acts only on larvae while they feed outside the stem. Slow, but kind to wasps and spiders.
The pyrethroid half kills spiders and can bring planthoppers back worse. Not for the first 40 days.
Works on borers, but very toxic to fish, shrimp and bees, and harsh on natural enemies. A last resort.
Kills spiders and wasps, and early use can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Highly toxic to people, fish, ducks and birds. A last resort only, and never near fishponds.
Kills spiders and wasps, and early use can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Hardly reaches larvae inside the stem, and kills the spiders that keep planthoppers down.
Hardly reaches larvae inside the stem, and is known to set off planthopper outbreaks.
Very toxic to fish, ducks and birds. A last resort only.

prevent: After harvest, plow and flood the field and cut stubble low, so the larvae resting in old stems die.
Plant in the same weeks as your neighbors and keep a fallow gap, so the moths find no young tillers between crops.
Pick egg masses off the seedlings before you pull them, and raise the water now and then to drown eggs laid low on the plant.
Split the nitrogen into doses. Heavy early nitrogen gives soft, lush tillers that the moths prefer.
Use a resistant or tolerant variety where your technician can supply one, and remove ratoons and volunteer rice.
bio: Egg wasps (Trichogramma, Telenomus, Tetrastichus) destroy many egg masses. Protect them by not spraying early.
Where Trichogramma cards are sold, pin them in the field when the moths start laying.
Spiders, lady beetles, ground beetles, earwigs and dragonflies eat the larvae and moths.
pests.threshold: From tillering, check 20 hills a week for egg masses and deadhearts, and run a light trap from panicle initiation. Act only when you find about 1 egg mass per square meter or deadhearts on 10 percent of tillers, and the egg jar test hatches more larvae than wasps.
pests.rotate: Striped stem borer in China now resists the diamides (IRAC 28) after years of heavy use. Do not use group 28 on two crops in a row. Switch with cartap (IRAC 14).

pests.name: Green leafhopper
pests.hint: Small green wedge shaped insects jump or run sideways when you disturb the hills.
pests.no: Sprays often fail to stop tungro. Ask a technician before you spray.

rice: Toxic to bees. A spray kills leafhoppers but cannot stop tungro once the virus is in.
Works on leafhoppers and brown planthopper alike. Toxic to bees. A spray cannot stop tungro once the virus is in.
Stops feeding. Better on planthoppers than on leafhoppers. Kind to spiders.
Kills nymphs only, not the adults that carry tungro. Slow but kind to spiders.
Still works on leafhoppers, though brown planthopper resists it. Toxic to bees.
Pyrethroids kill leafhoppers fast but also the spiders, and brown planthopper can come back worse.
Pyrethroids kill leafhoppers fast but also the spiders, and brown planthopper can come back worse.
Weak on leafhoppers. Keep it for stem borers and whorl maggot.
Highly toxic to people and harsh on natural enemies. A last resort only.
The pyrethroid half kills spiders and can bring brown planthopper back worse.
Very toxic to bees and harsh on spiders. A last resort.
Highly toxic to people, fish, ducks and birds. A last resort only, never near fishponds.
Kills spiders and mirid bugs and can set off brown planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Known to set off brown planthopper outbreaks. Very toxic to fish. A last resort.
Old carbamate. Leafhoppers in Asia have learned to survive this family. A last resort.
Very toxic to fish, ducks and birds. A last resort only.
A neem product. Mild and short lived on leafhoppers.
Known to set off brown planthopper outbreaks after spraying. A last resort.
Fipronil is very toxic to fish, shrimp and bees. Imidacloprid alone does the leafhopper job.
Old carbamate. Leafhoppers in Asia have learned to survive this family. A last resort.

prevent: Plant a tungro resistant or leafhopper resistant variety where tungro has struck before.
Plant at the same time across the barangay, and avoid the weeks when leafhoppers peaked in past seasons.
Transplant seedlings older than three weeks, and destroy stubble, ratoons and volunteer rice after harvest.
Use the right nitrogen rate, guided by the leaf color chart. Too much nitrogen invites outbreaks.
Keep weeds down, and run a light trap to see when the numbers rise.
bio: Spiders, dragonflies, damselflies and mirid bugs eat leafhoppers. Avoid early sprays so they stay.
Ducks in the paddy once the plants are well rooted eat leafhoppers along with planthoppers.
pests.threshold: Tap or sweep 20 hills a week in the first 40 days. A common action level is 2 leafhoppers per hill in tungro areas and 5 per hill elsewhere in the vegetative stage. In tungro areas a spray often fails to stop infection, so ask a technician first and pull yellowing hills at once.
pests.rotate: Green leafhoppers in East Asia resist many organophosphates and carbamates after decades of use. If an old product stops working, switch to group 4A, 9B or 4E, and do not repeat one group in a crop.

pests.name: Whitebacked planthopper
pests.hint: Small pale brown insects with a white stripe on the back sit low on the plant.

rice: Still works on this hopper, but it is toxic to bees. Use it once a crop, then switch to another group.
Same group 4A as thiamethoxam, so do not follow one with the other. Toxic to bees.
Kills the mirid bugs and egg wasps that hold this hopper down. One spray at most, late in the crop.

avoid: Cypermethrin
Pyrethroids kill the spiders and mirid bugs that eat hoppers, and planthoppers come back worse after the spray.
Lambda cyhalothrin plus thiamethoxam
The pyrethroid in it kills spiders and lets planthoppers come back worse.
Bifenthrin plus clothianidin
The pyrethroid in it kills spiders and lets planthoppers come back worse.
prevent: Plant within about three weeks of the farms around you, and grow no more than two rice crops a year.
Split the nitrogen into doses. Too much nitrogen, often on hybrid rice, builds up this hopper fast.
Drain the field for three to four days when the numbers climb.
Do not keep a ratoon crop, and plow the stubble in after harvest.
No insecticide in the first 30 to 40 days after transplanting unless the count passes the threshold.
bio: The mirid bug Cyrtorhinus lividipennis and Anagrus egg wasps are its main enemies. Broad spectrum sprays wipe them out.
Wolf spiders and lady beetles eat the nymphs. Count them with the hoppers before you decide.
pests.threshold: Count it with brown planthopper: tap 20 hills a week over the water from 30 days after transplanting. It peaks earlier, from tillering to booting. At 1 hopper per tiller or fewer do nothing. Consider a spray only near 25 hoppers per hill when hoppers outnumber spiders and mirid bugs.
pests.rotate: Whitebacked planthopper in East and Southeast Asia resists fipronil (IRAC 2B), so do not lean on it. Rotate among groups 4A, 9B and 16, and never use one group twice in a row.

pests.name: Rice whorl maggot
pests.hint: Yellow spots or streaks appear on the inner edges of new leaves.
pests.no: No spray is needed. The rice usually grows out of the damage.

rice: Rarely needed: rice outgrows this damage by maximum tillering. Use it only when a technician confirms heavy damage.
Rarely needed for whorl maggot. Worth it only when stem borers also need control.
Rarely needed: rice outgrows this damage by maximum tillering. Toxic to bees.
Highly toxic to people, fish, ducks and birds, and the damage seldom costs grain. A last resort only.
Kills the spiders and wasps of the young crop, and the damage seldom costs grain. A last resort.
Kills the spiders and wasps of the young crop, and the damage seldom costs grain. A last resort.
Kills the spiders and wasps of the young crop, and the damage seldom costs grain. A last resort.
Very toxic to fish, ducks and birds, and the damage seldom costs grain. A last resort only.
Kills the spiders and wasps of the young crop, and the damage seldom costs grain. A last resort.
Fipronil is very toxic to fish, shrimp and bees, far more than this pest calls for.

avoid: Deltamethrin
Early pyrethroid sprays kill spiders and set off planthopper outbreaks, for damage rice outgrows anyway.
Diazinon
An early spray known to set off planthopper outbreaks, for damage that rice outgrows anyway.
Beta cyfluthrin
Early pyrethroid sprays kill spiders and set off planthopper outbreaks, for damage rice outgrows anyway.
Alpha cypermethrin
Early pyrethroid sprays kill spiders and set off planthopper outbreaks, for damage rice outgrows anyway.
Lambda cyhalothrin plus thiamethoxam
The pyrethroid half kills the young crop's spiders and sets off planthopper outbreaks.
Chlorpyrifos plus cypermethrin
Kills the young crop's spiders and sets off planthopper outbreaks, for damage rice outgrows anyway.
Beta cypermethrin
Early pyrethroid sprays kill spiders and set off planthopper outbreaks, for damage rice outgrows anyway.
Bifenthrin plus imidacloprid
The pyrethroid half kills the young crop's spiders and sets off planthopper outbreaks.
Esfenvalerate
Early pyrethroid sprays kill spiders and set off planthopper outbreaks, for damage rice outgrows anyway.
Permethrin
Early pyrethroid sprays kill spiders and set off planthopper outbreaks, for damage rice outgrows anyway.
prevent: Expect some streaked, torn young leaves in flooded transplanted fields. It is not an emergency.
Keep every insecticide off the crop for the first 30 to 40 days, so spiders and wasps settle in for later pests.
Plant healthy, well rooted seedlings and give balanced fertilizer, so the crop outgrows the damage quickly.
Write down how many hills show damage in each lot, so you can tell a true outbreak from the usual few leaves.
bio: Small wasps attack the eggs and maggots, long legged flies eat the eggs, and spiders catch the adult flies.
pests.threshold: Check the youngest leaves of 20 hills in the first 30 days. Rice grows out of the damage by maximum tillering, so a spray almost never pays. Think of one only when more than about 20 percent of hills show fresh damage in a weak or late crop, and a technician agrees.

pests.name: Rice caseworm
pests.hint: Leaf tips are cut at right angles, as if with scissors.
pests.no: Drain the field first. If you must spray, use a carbamate, never a pyrethroid.

rice: Kind to spiders and wasps. Larvae stop feeding within a day but die over a few days. Drain the field first.
Breaks down in days, but it is toxic to fish. Drain the field first.
A carbamate, the usual answer for caseworm. Very toxic to bees and harsh on spiders. Drain first.
A carbamate that works on caseworm. Drain the field first. Spray only if cutting goes on.
Highly toxic to people and harsh on natural enemies. A last resort only.
The chlorpyrifos half kills spiders and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Highly toxic to people, fish, ducks and birds. A last resort only, never near fishponds.
Kills spiders and fish and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Known to set off planthopper outbreaks after spraying. A last resort.

avoid: Deltamethrin
Caseworm has grown tolerant of pyrethroids, and deltamethrin is known to set off planthopper outbreaks.
prevent: Drain the field for a few days when you see floating cases. Caseworms cannot move between hills without water.
Fix drainage so water does not stand long in low spots, where caseworm is worst.
Plant early, use wider spacing and transplant older seedlings, which suffer less.
Keep the bunds and canals free of weeds, and plant together with the farms around you.
Apply fertilizer at the rate your variety needs, not more.
bio: Water snails eat the eggs, water beetles eat the larvae, and spiders, dragonflies and birds catch the moths.
Ducks in the paddy pick up the floating cases.
pests.threshold: Check the seedbed and the first weeks of the crop for leaf tips cut square and for cases floating on the water. Drain the field for a few days first, since the larvae need standing water. Spray only if 1 to 2 live cases per hill remain and fresh cutting goes on after draining.
pests.rotate: Caseworm has grown tolerant of pyrethroids (IRAC 3A). If a spray is truly needed after draining, use a carbamate (1A) or tebufenozide (18).

pests.name: Rice hispa
pests.hint: White streaks run along the leaf, parallel to the midrib.
pests.no: No product names rice hispa on its label yet. Cultural steps and its natural enemies keep it down. Ask a technician before any spray.
prevent: Do not over fertilize. Heavily fertilized, lush fields draw the beetles.
Use the recommended spacing, not closer, so the leaves stay less dense.
Remove grassy weeds in the field and along the bunds and canals. They are the beetle's other hosts.
Sweep a net over the seedbed and the young crop to catch the adults while numbers are low.
Keep insecticides off the crop for the first 30 to 40 days, so the beetle's enemies stay.
bio: Small wasps attack the eggs and grubs inside the leaf, and reduviid bugs and spiders hunt the adults.
Fungi such as Beauveria and Metarhizium infect the beetles in humid weather.
pests.threshold: Walk the field before the end of tillering and count beetles, grubs and freshly streaked leaves on 20 hills. A common action level is 1 to 2 adults or freshly damaged leaves per hill. Below that, young rice regrows the lost leaf, and a technician should confirm before any spray.

pests.name: Rice armyworm
pests.hint: Leaves are chewed away, often including the veins, leaving only the midribs.
pests.no: Spray only at outbreak level, as the last resort.

rice: Kind to spiders and wasps. Caterpillars stop eating within a day but take a few days to die.
Fast on caterpillars, but kills spiders and is very toxic to fish. Early use can make planthoppers flare.
Fast on caterpillars, but kills spiders and is very toxic to fish. Early use can make planthoppers flare.
Highly toxic to people and harsh on natural enemies. A last resort only.
Weak on big caterpillars, and toxic to fish. A last resort.
Broad spectrum mix that kills spiders and wasps and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Kills spiders and fish and can set off planthopper outbreaks in rice. A last resort.
Broad spectrum mix that kills spiders and wasps and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Very toxic to bees and harsh on spiders. A last resort.
corn_yellow: Corn label. Kind to most natural enemies. Do not follow it with another group 28 product.
Broad spectrum mix that kills spiders and wasps and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Very toxic to bees and harsh on spiders. A last resort.
Kills spiders and fish and can set off planthopper outbreaks in rice. A last resort.
Corn seed treatment only. It guards seedlings for a few weeks and is weak on caterpillars.
corn_sweet: Corn label. Kind to most natural enemies. Do not follow it with another group 28 product.
Broad spectrum mix that kills spiders and wasps and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Very toxic to bees and harsh on spiders. A last resort.
Kills spiders and fish and can set off planthopper outbreaks in rice. A last resort.
Corn seed treatment only. It guards seedlings for a few weeks and is weak on caterpillars.
corn_glutinous: Corn label. Kind to most natural enemies. Do not follow it with another group 28 product.
Broad spectrum mix that kills spiders and wasps and can set off planthopper outbreaks. A last resort.
Very toxic to bees and harsh on spiders. A last resort.
Kills spiders and fish and can set off planthopper outbreaks in rice. A last resort.
Corn seed treatment only. It guards seedlings for a few weeks and is weak on caterpillars.

prevent: Set the seedbed far from weedy ground, and plow fallow land before the next crop.
Remove weeds, above all grasses, in and around the field and on the bunds.
Flood the seedbed when caterpillars appear. It is the best defense and drowns or drives them up for picking.
Dig a trench with ashes across the path of marching caterpillars, and lay branches around the field to collect them by hand.
Plow the field after harvest and keep checking weekly, so you see the first caterpillars while they are small.
bio: Wasps, tachinid flies, spiders and birds feed on armyworms. Early sprays kill them.
Where Bt or an armyworm virus (NPV) product is sold, aim it at young caterpillars.
pests.threshold: Check the seedbed and the young field every week, and every day after heavy rain that ends a dry spell. Spray only at outbreak level, when many caterpillars are marching in from one side and leaves are stripped to the midrib on large patches. Spray late in the afternoon, when the caterpillars come out to feed.

pests.name: Golden apple snail
pests.hint: Seedlings are cut at the base and the leaves float on the water.

rice: Fast, but very toxic to fish, frogs and native snails. Never let the treated water flow into canals or fishponds.
Gentler on fish than niclosamide and better where rain or strong irrigation may come. Pellets poison dogs, ducks and hens.
A plant product that breaks down within days, but it is also a fish poison. Keep fish and shrimp away from treated water.
The abamectin adds little against snails and more harm to fish and shrimp. Plain niclosamide does the same job.

prevent: Put wire or woven bamboo screens on the water inlet and outlet to keep snails and hatchlings out and to trap them.
At the last harrowing, dig small canals about 25 cm wide and 5 cm deep along the edges. Snails gather there when you drain.
Keep the water at 2 to 3 cm from 3 days after transplanting, and drain now and then. Level the field so no deep pockets stay.
Where snails are many, transplant older seedlings, about 25 to 30 days old, with stems too thick for the snail.
Hand pick snails in the morning and late afternoon, set bamboo stakes for them to lay on, and crush the pink egg masses.
Lay gabi, papaya or banana leaves in the canals as bait, then collect the snails that gather under them.
bio: Herd ducks into the field after harvest until the last harrowing, and again once the rice is past the danger stage. They eat young snails.
Red ants and long horned grasshoppers eat the eggs. Pick the big adults by hand, since ducks skip them.
Picked snails make duck or pig feed, or food when well cooked.
pests.threshold: Count snails and pink egg masses in the paddy and canals before you transplant. The danger window is the first 15 days after transplanting and the first 21 days after wet seeding. Rice about 30 days old resists the snail. Pick, drain and screen first, and treat only spots where snails stay many after that, the day after transplanting.

pests.hint: Tillers are cut at an angle and lie in the water, often in patches or in lines along the pilapil.
pests.no: No poison is recommended in rice. Work with your neighbors on the steps that do work.

prevent: Plant together: neighbors on about 10 hectares should plant in the same two weeks, so the crop ripens at once.
Keep pilapil and canal banks narrower than 20 cm and free of weeds, so rats cannot nest in them.
Clean up spilled grain, straw piles and rubbish at harvest. Sanitation is the longest lasting step.
Set a community trap barrier system: a 20 by 20 m plot planted 2 to 3 weeks early, fenced with plastic, with traps in the fence.
Dig out or flood burrows and hunt rats at night as a group at land preparation, before they breed.
If you bait, bait as a whole community, with sealed bait kept in stations for several days, never scattered once.
bio: Barn owls, grass owls, snakes and monitor lizards eat many rats. Perches and nest boxes near the field bring owls in.
Prefer traps and slow baits where owls hunt, since strong baits pass on to the owls that eat poisoned rats.
pests.threshold: Walk the pilapil and field edges every week from land preparation, looking for fresh burrows, runways and tillers cut at an angle. Act as a group at the first fresh signs. Bait works best from land preparation to maximum tillering, before the rats have grain. The trap barrier system pays off once damage reaches 10 percent.

pests.name: Mole cricket
pests.hint: Seedlings are cut at the base and bare patches show in the seedbed or field.
pests.no: No product names mole cricket on a rice label yet. Flooding, leveling and bund plastering do the work in rice.

corn_yellow: Corn seed treatment only: it guards the seedlings for their first weeks. Toxic to bees. Keep treated seed away from birds.
corn_sweet: Corn seed treatment only: it guards the seedlings for their first weeks. Toxic to bees. Keep treated seed away from birds.

prevent: Flood the field for 3 to 4 days before planting where you can. Water drives the crickets out and kills the eggs.
Level the field well, so it holds water evenly with no dry pockets for the crickets.
Shave the bunds and plaster them with fresh wet soil each season to kill eggs laid in the levees.
Pick nymphs and adults by hand during land preparation, and avoid dry, raised nursery beds.
In corn and upland fields, plow and harrow well before sowing so birds can pick the crickets from the turned soil.
bio: Sphecid wasps, carabid beetles, nematodes and fungi attack mole crickets, and the crickets eat each other.
Birds, frogs and ducks catch the crickets that flooding drives to the surface.
pests.threshold: Check the seedbed and the field at dusk and early morning for burrows, cut seedlings and bare patches, most often on high, dry spots. Flood and level first. Damage stops once the soil stays under water. Use a bait on the bunds only if cutting goes on after that.

pests.name: Rice birds (maya)
pests.local: Maya is the name for all four species. Mayang simbahan is the tree sparrow.
pests.hint: Flocks of small brown or chestnut birds land on the panicles at the milky stage.
pests.no: No spray or poison is advised. Bird poisons kill other birds and wildlife, and none is named for rice birds.
prevent: Plant together with the farms around you, so the ripening window is short and the flocks spread across many fields.
Guard the field at dawn and dusk from the milk stage to ripening, and change the scaring method often. Birds soon ignore one trick.
Net small plots and seedbeds where the crop is worth it. Only a net or a closed cover fully protects the grain.
Harvest on time, clean up spilled grain, and bird proof the grain store, where tree sparrows also live.
Cut tall weeds and bushes at the field edge where the birds roost.
bio: Leave egrets, herons, harriers and owls alone: they eat insects, frogs and rats, not grain.
pests.threshold: Watch the field at dawn and late afternoon from the milk stage to harvest and make sure the flock really feeds on the panicles. Start guarding at the first flocks. Birds that settle into a habit of one field are hard to move.

prevent: Plant at the same time as the farms around you, so the moths find no younger corn to move into.
Detassel 75 percent of plants at early tasseling, before pollen shed: keep one tasseled row in every four, and always detassel the first row.
Bury, burn or feed to animals the tassels you pull, and chop and plow under the stubble after harvest.
Plant a Bt corn hybrid where you can, since the corn borer is its main target, and keep scouting for the other pests.
bio: Trichogramma egg wasps stop borer eggs from hatching: release cards near day 28 to 30 and again near day 35 to 37.
Earwigs eat borer eggs and larvae: release colonies at mid whorl and at tasseling, and avoid sprays that kill them.
Bt and neem sprays kill young larvae in the whorl and spare the egg wasps.
pests.threshold: From about day 20 to silking, check 20 plants at each of five spots every week for egg masses under the leaves and pinholes in the whorl. Egg laying peaks near day 40 to 45. A whitefly and hopper product. Caterpillars like cutworms barely respond to it.
prevent: Plow and harrow two to three weeks before planting and keep the field weed free until then, so larvae starve and birds pick them out.
At dawn, dig around each freshly cut seedling and pick out the curled larva by hand.
Put a collar of paper, an old cup or bamboo around transplants of tomato, eggplant, pepper and cabbage.
Flood low fields for a few days before planting where water allows. It drives larvae up for birds or drowns them.
Pick egg masses and young leaf feeding colonies of common cutworm off the leaves by hand.
Light traps or sex pheromone traps catch moths and show when a new brood is coming.
bio: Ground beetles, earwigs, ants, spiders, toads and birds eat cutworms. Keep broad sprays out of the first weeks.
Bt kurstaki sprays kill young leaf feeding larvae, and Metarhizium or Beauveria on the soil infect the older ones.
Spodoptera litura NPV, where sold, kills common cutworm larvae and spares everything else.
pests.threshold: In the first three weeks, check 20 seedlings at each of five spots every two or three days, and dig around freshly cut plants at dawn to find the larva. pests.rotate: Common cutworm (Spodoptera litura) resists pyrethroids, organophosphates and carbamates in much of Asia, and in places emamectin and the diamides too. Rotate by generation among 28, 5 or 6, 22A, 15 and Bt, and never spray the same group twice in a row.

pests.threshold: Walk a W through the field each week from emergence to tasseling and check 10 plants at each of five stops. pests.rotate: Fall armyworm reached Asia carrying resistance to pyrethroids, organophosphates and carbamates, and some fields in China now respond less to chlorantraniliprole. prevent: Plow after harvest to break the pupal cells in the soil, and keep weeds and volunteer plants out of the field.
Plant corn at the same time as your neighbors, so silking does not drag on across the area.
Pick larvae by hand on small plots, and destroy bored fruits and ears so the larvae do not finish growing.
Plant a border of sunflower, marigold or castor around tomato and pepper as a trap crop, and spray or pick the larvae there.
A sex pheromone trap shows when moths arrive, so you know when to start checking silks and flowers.
bio: Trichogramma egg wasp cards cut earworm damage on corn in local trials. Release them as silking begins.
Spiders, lady beetles, assassin bugs and ants eat the eggs and young larvae. Skip pyrethroids to keep them.
Bt, neem and the fungi Beauveria and Metarhizium kill young larvae. Use them before any synthetic spray.
Helicoverpa NPV, where sold, kills the larvae and spares every natural enemy.
pests.threshold: From the first silks, check 20 ears at each of five spots twice a week for round white eggs and small larvae on the silks. On field corn a spray rarely pays. On sweet and glutinous corn sold fresh, act when 1 ear in 10 carries eggs or young larvae, in the first week of silking. On tomato, pepper and okra, check flowers and small fruits and act on young larvae before they bore in.
pests.rotate: Corn earworm (Helicoverpa armigera) resists pyrethroids across Asia through a gene now found almost everywhere, and in places resists organophosphates, carbamates and Bt cotton too. Rotate by generation, one group for about 30 days, among 28, 6, 22A, 5 and Bt, and never follow one group 28 product with another.

prevent: Pull out striped, stunted plants early: close the young leaves in your hand so hoppers cannot jump, bag the plant and burn it.

Rotate corn with a crop that is not a grass, so the hoppers lose their food between seasons.
Plant at the same time as your neighbors, and use virus resistant seed where it is sold.
bio: Spiders, lady beetles, mirid bugs that eat hopper eggs, and egg wasps keep numbers down. Avoid broad sprays that kill them.
Beauveria or Metarhizium fungus infects hoppers in humid weather.
pests.threshold: Each week check the whorls of 20 young plants at each of five spots, starting at the field edges where hoppers gather. Spray only when most young whorls hold many hoppers and new striped plants keep appearing. While striped plants stay near 1 to 2 percent, pull them out instead.

prevent: Collect the beetles by hand and with light traps for about three weeks from their first flight at the start of the rains, as a whole village.
Plow deep and harrow more than once. Pick up the grubs and let birds, earwigs and fire ants take the rest.
Time planting and cultivation to the beetle season, so young grubs meet freshly worked soil.
Flood the field for a few days where water allows. Grubs drown or come up for the birds.
Check the roots of a few wilting plants before you decide. Orange yellow patches that wilt are the sign.
bio: Scoliid wasps lay their eggs on the grubs, and ground beetles, birds, toads and fungus diseases kill many more.

pests.threshold: Before plowing and again in the first month, dig a square of soil one spade deep at ten spots per hectare and count the grubs, and check the roots of a few wilting plants. Treat in the furrow only where grubs turn up at most spots, timed for young grubs soon after the beetles fly with the first rains.

prevent: Weed the field and its edges. Grasses and weeds carry thrips into the crop.
Do not plant onion, garlic or melons beside an old crop of the same kind, and plant on the same dates as your neighbors.
Sprinkling from above washes thrips off onion leaves. Water this way in the dry months where you can.
Rice straw mulch on onion and garlic beds, and silver plastic mulch on sili and melons, cut thrips numbers.
Blue or yellow sticky traps at crop height show when thrips start to build up.
Remove or plow under old crop remains right after harvest.
bio: Minute pirate bugs, lacewings, predatory mites and predatory thrips eat thrips in fields that are not sprayed too often.
Beauveria bassiana or Metarhizium sprays help in humid weather. Aim them under the leaves and into the leaf folds.
pests.threshold: On onion and garlic, open the inner leaves of 20 plants at 5 spots: act at about 1 thrips per leaf on young plants, or 3 per leaf from bulbing. On sili, eggplant and melons, tap young shoots and flowers over white paper twice a week and act once young leaves begin to curl and most shoots carry thrips.
pests.rotate: Onion thrips and melon thrips in Asia survive pyrethroids, many organophosphates and carbamates, and often imidacloprid. Spinosad has failed where it was sprayed every week. Keep one group for a window of 2 to 3 weeks, then switch: spinosad or spinetoram (5), then abamectin (6) or cyantraniliprole (28), then a newer group such as flometoquin (34).

prevent: Raise seedlings under fine net and plant only clean seedlings, free of eggs and small larvae.
Plant the whole block at one time and leave a break of at least a month with no crucifer in the field.
Right after harvest, plow under or feed to animals the old stalks and leaves. Larvae and pupae live on in them.
Rotate cabbage, pechay and mustard with a crop of another family, such as tomato, beans or corn.
A row of mustard around the field draws the moths away from the cabbage. Destroy it once it fills with larvae.
Sprinkling the plants from above in the evening washes off young larvae and disturbs the moths.
bio: Protect the wasps Diadegma semiclausum in the highlands and Cotesia plutellae in the lowlands. Broad sprays kill them first.
Bt sprays (kurstaki or aizawai) kill only caterpillars and spare the wasps, spiders and syrphid flies.
Spiders, ground beetles and lacewings eat larvae and pupae left on the leaves.
pests.threshold: Check 20 plants at 5 spots twice a week from transplanting, looking under the leaves and in the heart. Act when 3 in 10 plants carry larvae before heading, or 1 in 10 once the heads form.
pests.rotate: Philippine moths resist pyrethroids, organophosphates and carbamates, moths in many Asian fields survive cartap, and moths on some highland farms survive every diamide. Keep one group for one window of about 3 to 4 weeks (one moth generation), then switch: Bt, then spinosad or spinetoram, then emamectin, then indoxacarb or chlorfenapyr, and drop any group that failed for the rest of the crop.

pests.name: Cabbage webworm
pests.hint: Silk webbing and frass sit in the heart of young plants.
pests.no: No product names the webworm on its label yet. Sprays you use for diamondback moth, such as Bt or spinosad, also hit it when they reach the heart of young plants.
prevent: Raise seedlings under fine net, in a seedbed kept clean of weeds and old crop remains.
Transplant strong seedlings about 5 to 6 inches tall. They outgrow early damage better.
Check the heart of each new transplant twice a week for two weeks. Crush larvae and pinch off damaged tips on small plots.
Clear crucifer weeds and old cabbage stalks, and plant the whole field at one time.
Webworm is worst in hot, dry spells. Sprinkling from above disturbs the moths and young larvae.
bio: The wasp Chelonus blackburni and other small wasps attack the eggs and larvae. Sprays that spare the diamondback moth wasps spare these too.
Bt aimed into the heart kills young larvae with no harm to the wasps.
pests.threshold: For the first month after transplanting, check the hearts of 20 plants at 5 spots twice a week for silk and fresh frass. Act when more than 1 in 20 hearts is webbed, since one larva in the growing point can kill the head.

pests.name: Onion armyworm

Lufenuron acts only on young larvae. Count the mix as a diamide window too.

prevent: Crush the white, cottony egg masses and the groups of tiny larvae (harabas) by hand while scouting.
Hang sex pheromone traps from transplanting and read them every few days to time your control.
Plant together with your neighbors, so no young onion field sits beside an old one full of larvae.
After harvest, clear weeds and old leaves, then plow or flood the field so the pupae in the soil die.
Rest the field from onion and other hosts for a season. Rice after onion breaks the cycle well.
Light traps at night, or fine net over small shallot plots, keep the moths off.
bio: Spiders, earwigs and predatory wasps eat eggs and larvae. Pyrethroid sprays kill them first.
The beet armyworm virus (SeNPV) and Bt aizawai, where you can buy them, work best on newly hatched larvae.
pests.threshold: From 2 weeks after transplanting, check 20 plants at 5 spots twice a week for white, cottony egg masses and groups of tiny larvae. Crush them by hand. Spray only when young larvae show in many spots after handpicking, or when pheromone trap catches jump.
pests.rotate: Beet armyworm in Asia resists pyrethroids, organophosphates and carbamates, and in China many fields now resist diamides and some resist emamectin. Use one group per generation, about 3 to 4 weeks: a diamide (28), then emamectin (6), then spinosad (5) or indoxacarb (22A).

prevent: Clip wilted shoot tips and bored fruits every week, bag them and bury them deep. Never leave them on the ground.
Raise seedlings under fine net and plant only seedlings with clean, unbored tips.
Hang sex pheromone traps from transplanting to the last harvest, and change the lure on time.
After the last picking, uproot and destroy the old plants. Do not set a new field beside an old one.
Rotate with a crop outside the eggplant family, such as corn, rice or beans, and remove wild nightshade weeds.
Grow a variety with better borer tolerance where one is available.
bio: Earwigs, the wasp Trathala flavoorbitalis and egg wasps attack the borer. Early broad sprays kill them.
Trichogramma cards placed weekly from flowering cut the number of eggs that hatch.
Bt sprays reach only newly hatched larvae before they bore in. Time them with the trap catch.
pests.threshold: Walk the field weekly from 2 weeks after transplanting, check 20 plants and clip every wilted tip and bored fruit. Spray only when fresh damage still shows on more than 5 in 100 shoots or fruits after clipping, or when the pheromone trap catch climbs two weeks in a row.
pests.rotate: In South Asia the borer resists pyrethroids and organophosphates. Rotate by windows of about 4 weeks: a diamide (28), then spinosad or spinetoram (5), then emamectin (6) or indoxacarb (22A), and come back to a group only after the others.

pests.threshold: From flowering, check 20 young fruits at 5 spots twice a week for sting marks, and read cue lure traps weekly. Start weekly bait sprays as soon as traps catch flies every week or the first stings show. By the time fruit rots, it is too late.
