Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
tamarind: Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
coffee: Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
mango: Old broad carbamate, toxic to people, bees and fish. A last resort with the full waiting time.
Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
dragonfruit: Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
rambutan: Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
Hits only the moving crawlers. Covered scales survive, and it kills the wasps that keep scales down.
banana: Works on the crawlers and young scales only. Time it to the crawler stage. It can harm lady beetle larvae.
A soap: it kills only the young crawlers it wets, so spray when they hatch and cover well.

prevent: Prune and burn or bury twigs and branches crusted with scales, and open the crown to light and wind.
Check seedlings, budwood and cuttings before planting. Scales arrive on planting material and on wind blown crawlers.
Keep ants off the trunks with sticky bands. Ants guard soft scales and chase away their enemies.
Water and feed trees well in the dry season. Scales build up on stressed, dusty trees.
Keep road dust down and avoid broad sprays. Both kill the tiny wasps that keep scales low.
A light oil spray on the crawlers, where an oil product is labeled for the crop, spares most natural enemies.
bio: Tiny wasps such as Aphytis and Comperiella parasitize scales. A small round hole in a scale cover means a wasp came out.
Lady beetles such as Chilocorus and their spiny larvae eat many scales. Protect them by spraying less.
The fungus Lecanicillium lecanii often wipes out green scale on coffee and citrus in wet months.
pests.threshold: Each month, and every two weeks in the dry season, look at 10 twigs, leaves and fruits on 10 trees per block. Spray only where live scales crowd twigs or fruit and few covers show the small round exit hole of a wasp. Time it to the crawler stage, when tiny moving yellow specks show on tape wrapped around a twig.

pests.name: Spiraling whitefly
pests.hint: White waxy spirals of eggs and fluffy white nymphs cover the underside of leaves, with sticky honeydew and black sooty mold on top.

sources.label: CBSUA, The spiralling whitefly, a Philippine perspective
Pacific Pests and Pathogens, Spiralling whitefly

prevent: Wash colonies off the leaf undersides with a strong water jet each week in the dry season.
Prune and bag heavily infested leaves and twigs, and do not move infested plants or cuttings.
Water and mulch trees in the dry season. Outbreaks build on dusty, water stressed plants.
Keep ants down. They guard the nymphs from wasps and lady beetles.
Avoid broad sprays such as pyrethroids and organophosphates. They wipe out the wasps and outbreaks come back worse.
bio: Tiny Encarsia wasps and the small lady beetle Nephaspis keep spiraling whitefly low where they are established.
Lacewing larvae and spiders also feed on the nymphs. Most outbreaks fade once the enemies catch up.
pests.threshold: In the dry season, check the undersides of 10 leaves on 10 plants each week. Before any action, look for black, parasitized nymphs: if many are black, the wasps are winning. Wash or prune when spirals and fluffy nymphs cover many leaves and sooty mold spreads.

pests.name: Asian citrus psyllid
pests.hint: Small brown jumping bugs and their nymphs with white waxy threads crowd on new flushes, which curl and twist, and they spread citrus greening.

sources.label: Philippine Agricultural Scientist, HLB and tristeza in Oriental Mindoro calamansi
ATI 4B, Calamansi production guide

prevent: Buy only certified disease free seedlings grown under screen. Greening and psyllids arrive on planting material.
Kill the psyllids on trees with greening, then cut and destroy those trees, so the insects do not carry it on.
Take out kamuning (Murraya) hedges near citrus. It is a favorite host of the psyllid.
Time pruning and fertilizer so the whole orchard flushes at once, and guard that young flush, where the psyllids breed.
Work as a whole area with the neighbors. Psyllids fly from orchard to orchard.
bio: The tiny wasp Tamarixia radiata parasitizes psyllid nymphs. Avoid broad sprays so it survives.
Lady beetles, lacewings, hoverfly larvae and spiders eat nymphs on the young flush.
Beauveria bassiana and Isaria fumosorosea infect psyllids in humid weather.
pests.threshold: Each week while trees flush, look at 10 new shoots on 10 trees per block for yellow nymphs with white waxy threads, and tap branches over a white board for adults. Near trees with greening, act on any psyllid you find. Elsewhere act when nymphs show on many flushes.
pests.rotate: Psyllids in Florida and parts of Asia lost sensitivity to imidacloprid and other neonicotinoids after heavy use. Do not give the same neonicotinoid flush after flush. Alternate with oil.

pests.name: Citrus rind borer
pests.hint: Small caterpillars tunnel in the rind of young fruits, leaving gummy entry holes and corky scars, and many fruits rot or drop.

sources.label: UPLB, Citrus rind borer Prays endolemma on pummelo

pomelo: Reaches only newly hatched larvae on the skin, not those in the rind. Kills bees and natural enemies. Bagging works better.
Old, toxic organophosphate. A last resort only, with the full waiting time before harvest.
calamansi: Reaches only newly hatched larvae on the skin, not those in the rind. Kills bees and natural enemies. Bagging works better.
Old, toxic organophosphate. A last resort only, with the full waiting time before harvest.
citrus: Reaches only newly hatched larvae on the skin, not those in the rind. Kills bees and natural enemies. Bagging works better.
Old, toxic organophosphate. A last resort only, with the full waiting time before harvest.

avoid: Imidacloprid
Does little to caterpillars inside the rind. It is made for sucking insects such as scales and mealybugs.
prevent: Bag pomelo fruits soon after fruit set and thinning, with net or paper bags. In trials bagging was the most cost effective control.
Pick off and bury fruits with rind lumps, and gather fallen fruits every week, so larvae cannot finish their growth.
Thin fruit clusters so each fruit can be checked and bagged.
Prune trees low and open so bagging, picking and checks are quick.
Work with your neighbors. An unbagged orchard nearby keeps the moth going.
bio: Entomopathogenic fungi sprayed on young fruits cut rind lumps to a small share of fruits in a mandarin trial.
Tiny egg wasps, spiders and ants attack eggs and young larvae on the skin. Broad sprays kill them.
pests.threshold: From fruit set, check 20 young fruits on each of 10 trees every week for tiny gummy specks or raised lumps on the rind. Eggs go on the skin as early as fruit set and the cycle takes about 3 weeks, so bag at once when the first marks show.
pests.rotate: In a mandarin trial, fruits sprayed with chlorpyrifos still showed over a quarter with rind lumps, a sign the moth may be learning to survive sprays. Do not lean on one group. Bagging and fungi cut damage more.

pests.name: Citrus bark borer
pests.hint: Zigzag tunnels, cuts and rough edges show on the bark with oozing gum, and branches above the damage wilt and dry.
pests.no: Sprays do not reach the grubs under the bark. Cut out and burn infested branches and keep trees vigorous.

sources.label: ATI 4B, Calamansi production guide

prevent: Cut off branches with wilting leaves and zigzag tunnels well below the damage, and burn them before the adults come out.
At each fresh gum spot, open the bark with a sharp knife, kill the grub in its tunnel, and seal the wound.
Keep trees vigorous with water in the dry season and balanced fertilizer. The beetles favor stressed, weak trees.
Avoid wounding the trunk with tools, and clear old, dying citrus trees near the orchard that breed the beetle.
bio: Woodpeckers, ants and small wasps take grubs and eggs on the bark. Do not spray trunks needlessly.
pests.threshold: Every month, walk around each tree and look at the trunk and main branches for fresh gum oozing from the bark and zigzag ridges under it. Act on every tree with fresh gum. One borer can girdle a branch.

pests.name: Buff coconut mealybug
pests.hint: Buff colored mealybugs with short waxy filaments pack on fruits, leaves and twigs, fruits stay small and black with sooty mold, and trees decline.

sources.label: UPLB, Rehabilitating mealybug infested atis in Lobo, Batangas

prevent: Bag atis and guyabano fruits early with paper or net bags. It keeps crawlers and the ants that carry them off.
Cut off and bag infested fruits and shoots, and gather fallen fruits, before crawlers spread.
Keep ants off the trunk with sticky bands and break their nests near the trees.
Check seedlings and scions before planting, and clean tools and sacks after working an infested tree.
Wash small colonies off with a strong jet of water.
bio: The tiny wasp Pseudaphycus utilis has brought buff coconut mealybug under control elsewhere. Protect wasps by spraying less.
Lady beetles such as the mealybug destroyer, lacewings and hoverfly larvae eat the colonies.
pests.threshold: Each week look at 10 fruits and shoot tips on 10 trees. Cut out or wash off single colonies. Act on the block when colonies spread to many fruits and you see few brown, puffed parasitized mealybugs.

pests.name: Red branch borer (carpenter moth)
pests.hint: Pinkish red caterpillars tunnel inside branches and young stems, pushing sawdust out of small holes, and the part above wilts and dies.
pests.no: Sprays do not reach the caterpillar inside the branch. Cut off wilted branches below the hole, or kill it with a wire.

sources.label: BPI, Cacao production guide
BPI, Durian production guide

prevent: Cut wilted branches a hand's width below the lowest hole and burn them with the caterpillar inside.
In thick branches you want to keep, push a flexible wire into the hole to kill the caterpillar, then plug the hole with mud or wax.
Prune and keep trees vigorous. Young trees and weak shoots suffer most.
Clear dead and dying branches and wild hosts near the farm, where the moth breeds.
Check new trees from the nursery for holes and sawdust before planting.
bio: Birds, ants and parasitic wasps take many eggs and young caterpillars before they bore in.
Beauveria bassiana pushed into the holes on a wet cotton plug can infect the caterpillar inside.
pests.threshold: Each week look for wilting tips and small holes pushing out fresh reddish sawdust on branches and young stems. Act on every hole you find. One caterpillar kills the whole branch above it.

pests.name: Mosquito bug (Helopeltis)
pests.hint: Dark sunken spots and scabby lesions appear on young pods, shoots and nuts where the slender red and black bugs feed, and shoots dry out.

sources.label: BPI, Cacao production guide
Helopeltis mosquito bugs, species in the Philippines

cacao: Old broad spray that kills the black ants and weaver ants that guard pods. Spot spray hot spots only.
Old, toxic organophosphate. Spot spray hot spots only, with the full waiting time before harvest.

prevent: Harvest pods on time and remove damaged and black pods, so bugs have fewer young pods to feed on.
Prune water sprouts and thin the canopy and shade so trees are not dark and damp, where the bugs build up.
Watch most closely during flushing and early pod or nut growth, when damage hurts most.
Clear wild hosts of the bug near the farm, and do not plant guava, cashew and cacao side by side without checking all three.
Spot spray only the trees with fresh damage, not the whole farm, so the ants stay.
bio: Black cocoa ants and weaver ants (hantik) drive the bugs off pods. Help them nest in the trees and keep sprays off them.
Assassin bugs, spiders and Beauveria bassiana also kill Helopeltis in humid weather.
pests.threshold: Each week look at the young pods, shoots and nuts of 20 trees, early in the morning when the bugs feed. Fresh dark water soaked spots on many young pods or new cashew shoots in one week mean act. Old dry scabs do not.

pests.name: Banana leaf roller (banana skipper)
pests.hint: Leaf edges are cut and rolled into tubes, each with a caterpillar covered in white powder inside.

sources.label: DA HVCDP, Giya sa Pagpananum ug Abaca (Technoguide 05, 2019)

banana: Old broad spray that kills the wasps parasitizing the skipper. Pick off leaf rolls first.

prevent: Pick off and crush the leaf rolls with the caterpillar or pupa inside. On small farms this is often enough.
Cut off and burn badly rolled and torn leaf parts, and remove old dry leaves where pupae hide.
Check young plants and suckers every week, since big caterpillars strip a leaf to the midrib in days.
Keep the plantation weeded and desuckered so leaves are easy to see and reach.
bio: Egg wasps (Ooencyrtus), larval wasps (Cotesia) and Brachymeria parasitize the skipper. Broad sprays kill them.
Bt sprays on the fresh rolls kill young caterpillars and spare these wasps.
pests.threshold: Each week walk 20 mats per block and count fresh leaf rolls with a live caterpillar inside. Act when fresh rolls show on many plants, while the caterpillars are still small. Old torn leaves with empty rolls need nothing.

pests.name: Atis and guyabano fruit borer
pests.hint: Caterpillars bore into the fruit, leaving holes with brown frass and webbing, and the flesh inside turns black and rots.

sources.label: FAO AGRIS, Control measures for atis fruit borer

prevent: Bag atis and guyabano fruits soon after fruit set with paper, net or perforated plastic bags. It is the control that works.
Pick off and bury bored fruits, and gather fallen fruits every few days, so the caterpillars cannot pupate.
Thin fruits so they do not touch. Caterpillars often move from fruit to fruit where they press together.
Prune trees low and open so fruits are easy to bag and check.
Harvest on time and leave no overripe fruits on the tree.
bio: Egg wasps, ants and spiders attack eggs and young caterpillars on the fruit skin. Avoid broad sprays.
pests.threshold: Each week look at 20 young fruits per tree for small holes with brown frass and webbing. Bag all fruits before the first holes show. Once a caterpillar is inside, the fruit is lost.

pests.name: Banana flower thrips and red rust thrips
pests.hint: Young fingers get tiny black specks that grow into rough corky scab, or reddish brown rust where fingers touch, and badly hit fruit splits open.

sources.label: BPI, Banana production guide
DA HVCDP, Banana production manual

banana: Spray the young bunch as the bracts lift. Kind to most predators, but keep it off bees while wet.
Toxic to bees and fish. Aim it at the young bunch only.
Toxic to fish and birds. Use it once in a rotation, not bunch after bunch.
A treated bunch bag put on early. The bag guards the fingers without a spray.
Highly toxic to people and to natural enemies. A last resort with full protective clothing.
Old organophosphate being phased out in many countries. Mostly used in treated bunch bags.
Never inject it into the banana bud, which is banned. Very toxic to fish and bees.
Weak on thrips. It works better on aphids and mealybugs.

avoid: Deltamethrin
Banned on banana.
prevent: Bag each bunch soon after it shoots. A plain bag alone already cuts scab and rust.
Cut off the male bud and brush away the dry bracts and dead flowers on the fingers early. Thrips hide and breed in them.
Keep flowering weeds down in the plantation. Flower thrips breed on weed flowers too.
Desucker and deleaf on time so bunches dry fast and any spray reaches the young hands.
Plant clean suckers or tissue cultured plantlets with no soil on them. Rust thrips pupate in the soil and travel with it.
Spray, if you must, only the young bunch, not the whole plant, so natural enemies survive.
bio: Minute pirate bugs, predatory thrips, lacewings and spiders eat thrips. Whole plant broad sprays kill them.
Beauveria bassiana or Metarhizium on young bunches can cut thrips numbers in humid weather.
pests.threshold: At shooting, open the bracts of 10 new bunches per block and look for thrips with a hand lens. Check the young fingers again a week later. Flower thrips do their damage in the first 2 weeks after the bunch shows, so protect every bunch from shooting. Rust thrips show later where fingers touch.
pests.rotate: Thrips soon learn to survive a group used bunch after bunch, and flower thrips in Asia resist pyrethroids, organophosphates and even spinosad in places. Rotate spinosad (5), abamectin (6), chlorfenapyr (13) and spirotetramat (23), and never repeat one group on back to back bunch cycles.

pests.name: Mango seed borer (red banded mango caterpillar)
pests.hint: Caterpillars bore in near the tip of young fruits and eat the flesh and seed, leaving holes that ooze, and the fruits crack, rot and drop.

sources.label: DA Caraga HVCDP, Giya sa pagpananum ug manga

mango: Old broad carbamate, toxic to people, bees and fish. A last resort with the full waiting time.

prevent: Bag the fruits during growth. Eggs go on the fruit stalk and base, and newly hatched caterpillars bore in from the side.
Pick off and destroy fruits with dark stains every week. They hold the caterpillars.
In the off season, gather and burn dead wood and scrape loose bark, where the caterpillars pupate.
Keep anthracnose low. Moths also lay eggs in the cracks of anthracnose spots.
Leave weaver ants on the trees. In one trial a broad spray that killed them gave more damage than no spray.
bio: Two egg wasps, Trichogramma chilonis and Trichogramma chilotraeae, attack the eggs in the Philippines. Spare them.
Weaver ants (hantik) catch the moths. Neem sprays every 10 days from flowering cut damage in one country.
pests.threshold: From about 45 days after flower induction, check 20 fruits per tree on 10 trees each week for a dark sticky stain running down from a hole near the stalk end. Act at the first stains: pick off those fruits and bag the rest.

pests.name: Jackfruit shoot and fruit borer
pests.hint: Caterpillars bore into flower spikes, shoots and young fruits, leaving holes with brown frass, and the fruits rot or drop.

sources.label: Philstar, Filipino scientists test Metarhizium on jackfruit borer
Vikaspedia, IPM for jackfruit pests

prevent: Bag or wrap young fruits in sacks, net or perforated plastic soon after fruit set.
Gather fallen male flower spikes and bored fruits every few days and bury or burn them. The caterpillars breed in them.
Cut off and burn bored shoots well below the hole.
Thin crowded fruits so each can be bagged and checked.
Prune trees open and low enough to reach the fruits for bagging.
bio: Egg wasps, ants and spiders attack the eggs and young caterpillars. Avoid broad sprays.
Bt sprays on young fruits and spikes kill small caterpillars before they bore in.
pests.threshold: Each week check young fruits, flower spikes and new shoots of every tree for holes with brown frass. Bag fruits before the first holes appear, and cut out bored shoots and spikes as you find them.

pests.name: Jackfruit fruit fly
pests.hint: Flies sting the rind of maturing fruits, maggots feed inside, and the flesh under the sting marks turns soft and rotten.

sources.label: Vikaspedia, IPM for jackfruit pests

prevent: Wrap each fruit in a sack, net or plastic bag while still young and firm, and keep it on until harvest.
Gather and bury fallen and rotting fruits every few days, so the maggots cannot pupate in the soil.
Harvest at maturity and do not leave ripe fruits on the tree.
Kill the males with methyl eugenol blocks or wicks spread through the area. This fly comes to that lure.
Clear unpicked breadfruit and jackfruit near the farm and work with the neighbors.
bio: Native wasps parasitize the eggs and maggots inside the fruit. They survive where cover sprays are few.
Weaver ants, other ants and chickens take maggots and pupae under the trees.
pests.threshold: Hang methyl eugenol traps in the orchard and count the males each week. When the catch climbs as fruits near maturity, check every unbagged fruit for sting marks with oozing sap, and bag or pick at once.

pests.name: Avocado twig borers
pests.hint: Beetle larvae bore into twigs and small branches, which wilt, dry and break off.
pests.no: Sprays do not reach the grubs inside the twigs. Cut infested twigs below the damage and burn them.

sources.label: FAO, Avocado production in the Philippines

prevent: Cut wilted and bored twigs well below the lowest hole and burn them with the grub inside.
Clear dead branches, prunings and brush piles from the orchard. The beetles breed in dead and dying wood.
Check the trees most closely during flushing, when the beetles lay eggs on young twigs.
Keep trees vigorous with water in the dry season and balanced fertilizer.
Look over grafted seedlings for bored twigs before planting.
bio: Birds, ants and small parasitic wasps take many eggs and young grubs. Do not spray the canopy needlessly.
pests.threshold: After each flush, look over every tree for wilting twig tips, small holes and fine sawdust. Act on each wilted twig as you find it. There is no count to wait for.

pests.name: Lanzones scale
pests.hint: Leaves get crowded with tiny white and brown scales, yellow and drop early, fruits stay few, small and sour, and badly hit trees can die.
pests.no: Sprays have done poorly against it. Prune and burn heavily infested branches, feed and water trees well, and protect the lady beetles that eat the scales.

sources.label: Zootaxa, Unaspis lansivora, a new scale pest of lanzones in the Philippines
GMA News, Chemicals no match for lanzones pest

avoid: Malathion
Lanzones scales sit under a hard cover it barely reaches, and it kills the Chilocorus lady beetles released against them.
Fenitrothion
Lanzones scales sit under a hard cover it barely reaches, and it kills the Chilocorus lady beetles released against them.
prevent: Prune and burn branches heavy with scales, and open the crown and the shade trees above it to light and air.
Feed and water trees well, mostly in the dry season. Badly hit trees recover only when they are strong.
Do not carry lanzones seedlings, scions or cut branches from an infested farm to a clean one.
Keep broad sprays out of the orchard so the lady beetles and wasps can build up.
Check the trees after every harvest and treat new hot spots early, before the whole tree is crusted.
bio: The lady beetle Chilocorus nigrita eats lanzones scales well and is mass reared for lanzones farms in Mindanao. Ask for releases.
Tiny parasitic wasps also attack the scales. A scale with a small round hole means one came out.
pests.threshold: Each month look at 10 leaves and twigs on each of 10 trees. Act on any tree where scales crowd the leaves or leaves start to yellow and drop: prune the worst branches and ask for lady beetle releases.

pests.name: Lanzones bark borer
pests.hint: Larvae feed under the bark of the trunk and main branches, leaving frass and dead, peeling bark patches, and weak trees bear less.

sources.label: BPI, Lanzones production guide

lanzones: Two old broad insecticides. Brush it only on scraped, infested bark patches, never over the whole tree.

prevent: Scrape off dead, peeling bark with frass down to clean wood, kill the larvae you find, and burn the scrapings.
Cut off and burn dead branches, and do not pile prunings near the trees.
Keep trees vigorous: feed, water in the dry season, and prune shade so the trunk dries.
Avoid wounding the bark with ladders, ropes and bolos at harvest. Borers enter through wounds.
Check every tree after harvest, when weakened trees are most often attacked.
bio: Ants, birds and Beauveria or Metarhizium fungi kill larvae under the bark in wet weather. Avoid broad trunk sprays.
pests.threshold: Each month look at the trunk and main branches of every tree for fine frass, wet dark spots and dead, peeling bark. Act on each patch as you find it, before it rings the trunk.

pests.name: Durian fruit borer
pests.hint: Caterpillars bore into young and growing fruits through the stalk, base or side, leaving holes with frass, and fruits rot or drop.

sources.label: BPI, Durian production guide
DA HVCDP and BPI DNCRDC, Durian production guide

prevent: Thin fruit clusters so fruits do not touch, or slip a piece of sack or foam between them. Borers enter where fruits press together.
Pick off and bury bored and fallen fruits every week, so the caterpillars cannot pupate.
Wrap young fruits in net bags where labor allows.
Prune the canopy open so fruits are easy to reach, check and treat.
Clear wild hosts of the shoot and fruit borer near the orchard, such as castor and unpicked fruits.
bio: Egg wasps, ants and spiders attack eggs and young caterpillars on the fruit. Avoid broad sprays.
Bt sprays on young fruits kill small caterpillars before they bore in.
pests.threshold: From 2 weeks after fruit set, check every fruit cluster each week, mostly where fruits touch and at the stalk, for small holes with wet brown frass. Act at the first fresh holes: remove bored fruits and treat or wrap the rest.

pests.name: Durian psyllids (including bao bao)
pests.sci: Allocaridara malayensis (also written Allocarsidara incognita), Haplaphalara sp.
pests.hint: Tiny sap sucking bugs swarm on new flushes, leaves curl, yellow and dry, white waxy threads appear, and flowers and fruitlets drop.

sources.label: BPI, Durian production guide
DA HVCDP and BPI DNCRDC, Durian production guide

avoid: Dimethoate
Old, toxic organophosphate with no label for this pest. The other choices are safer.
prevent: Time pruning and fertilizer so each tree flushes all at once, and guard that young flush, where the psyllids breed.
Cut off and burn heavily infested flush tips early, before the nymphs mature.
Do not overfeed with nitrogen. Soft, repeated flushes feed more psyllids.
Water trees in the dry season and keep them healthy, so they hold flowers and fruitlets under attack.
Spray, if you must, only the young flush, not the whole tree, so the natural enemies survive.
bio: Lacewings, lady beetles, spiders and small parasitic wasps eat psyllid nymphs on the flush. Avoid broad sprays.
Beauveria bassiana infects psyllids in humid weather.
pests.threshold: Each week while trees flush and set fruit, look at 10 new shoots on 10 trees for tiny nymphs, white waxy threads and curling leaves. Act when nymphs crowd many young flushes. Rainy spells and new flush bring them up fast.

pests.name: Shot hole borer
pests.hint: Tiny black or brown beetles drill many pinholes in the trunk and main branches of stressed trees, often together with Phytophthora canker.
pests.no: Sprays do not reach the beetles in the wood. Keep trees vigorous, treat canker and burn heavily bored wood.

sources.label: BPI, Durian production guide

prevent: Treat Phytophthora canker on the trunk early. The beetles come to trees already sick or stressed.
Cut and burn heavily bored branches and dead trees at once, before the new beetles leave them.
Keep trees vigorous: good drainage, mulch, water in the dry season and balanced fertilizer.
Avoid trunk wounds from tools and ladders, and seal pruning cuts.
Do not stack fresh cut durian or other wood near the orchard. It draws and breeds the beetles.
pests.threshold: Each month look at the trunk and main branches for clusters of pinholes with fine sawdust, often near cankers that ooze. A few holes on a weak tree mean fix its stress now. Holes all over a dying branch mean cut it.

pests.name: Tussock caterpillars
pests.hint: Hairy caterpillars with tufts on the back eat young flushes and leaves, leaving ragged leaves; the hairs can sting the skin.

sources.label: BPI, Mangosteen production guide
DA HVCDP, Mangosteen production guide

avoid: Carbaryl
Kills bees and the wasps that parasitize tussock caterpillars, and can bring mites and scales after it.
prevent: Wear gloves and pick off the hairy egg masses and the young caterpillar groups, then crush or burn them.
Cut off and burn twigs with webbing and caterpillar groups.
Tie sticky bands around the trunk to catch caterpillars and wingless females climbing up.
Check the trees most closely at each flush. The caterpillars go for young leaves.
Keep the hairs off skin and eyes: work in long sleeves and do not burn the hairs where smoke blows on people.
bio: Parasitic wasps and flies, birds and a natural virus often crash tussock caterpillar outbreaks. Avoid broad sprays.
Bt sprays on young caterpillars kill them and spare their enemies.
pests.threshold: Each week while trees flush, look over the new leaves for hairy egg masses and groups of small caterpillars. Remove them by hand while they are still together. Spray only when many trees carry big, spread out caterpillars.

pests.name: Moringa leaf caterpillar
pests.hint: Small green caterpillars web and scrape the leaflets until only the veins are left, and whole trees can be stripped bare in the dry season.

sources.label: Diseases and pests of moringa, a mini review

prevent: Pick and destroy webbed leaves with the caterpillars inside, early, while few trees are hit.
Cut back badly hit branches hard. Malunggay sprouts back fast with clean leaves.
Loosen the soil under the trees after an attack, so the pupae there dry out or are eaten.
Harvest leaves often and keep trees low. Frequent cuts leave the caterpillars little to feed on.
Leaves are eaten fresh, so avoid chemical sprays. Use the steps above and Bt.
bio: Bt sprays on young caterpillars kill them and leave the leaves safe to eat after a short wait.
Spiders, wasps and chickens under the trees eat many caterpillars and pupae.
pests.threshold: In the dry season, look at the leaves of every tree twice a week for webbing and scraped leaflets. Act at the first webs, because a heavy brood can strip a tree in a week.

pests.name: Tamarind seed beetle
pests.hint: Small brown beetles and their grubs bore into the pods and seeds, leaving round exit holes and powder, and the damage keeps growing in stored pods.
pests.no: Sprays do not reach grubs inside pods and seeds. Sun dry, shell and seal tamarind in airtight containers.

sources.label: TNAU Agritech Portal, Tamarind

avoid: Quinalphos
Old toxic organophosphate with no label for this beetle. Sprays do not reach grubs inside pods and seeds.
prevent: Harvest pods as soon as they ripen. Do not leave them hanging long or lying on the ground.
Sun dry the pods well, then shell them and take out the seeds. The grubs grow inside the seeds.
Store the pulp and any seeds kept in airtight jars or sealed bags, away from old stock.
Throw out or burn infested pods and clean the storeroom before the new harvest comes in.
Small lots can be frozen for a few days to kill eggs and grubs before storing.
pests.threshold: At harvest and every month in storage, open 20 pods or a handful of seeds and look for round exit holes, powder and grubs. Any live beetle in storage means sort, dry and reseal the stock at once.

diseases.name: Sheath blight
diseases.hint: Oval, gray green spots on the sheath near the water that climb the plant.

rice: Aim the spray at the lower sheaths, where the disease starts. Do not use group 11 twice in a row.
Aim the spray at the lower sheaths, where the disease starts. Do not use group 11 twice in a row.
A strobilurin used alone: rotate it with a triazole so the fungus does not learn to survive it.
Older and weaker than the triazoles on sheath blight, and many fungi have learned to survive this group.
Only partial control of sheath blight. The triazole mixes do better.
Older and weaker than the triazole mixes on sheath blight. A second line choice.
A friendly bacterium. It slows the disease a little but will not stop lesions climbing in wet weather.
corn_yellow: Aim the spray at the lower sheaths, where the disease starts. Do not use group 11 twice in a row.
A strobilurin used alone: rotate it with a triazole so the fungus does not learn to survive it.
A strobilurin used alone: rotate it with a triazole so the fungus does not learn to survive it.
corn_sweet: Aim the spray at the lower sheaths, where the disease starts. Do not use group 11 twice in a row.
A strobilurin used alone: rotate it with a triazole so the fungus does not learn to survive it.
A strobilurin used alone: rotate it with a triazole so the fungus does not learn to survive it.
corn_glutinous: Aim the spray at the lower sheaths, where the disease starts. Do not use group 11 twice in a row.
A strobilurin used alone: rotate it with a triazole so the fungus does not learn to survive it.
A strobilurin used alone: rotate it with a triazole so the fungus does not learn to survive it.

avoid: Copper hydroxide
Copper does not control the sheath blight fungus.
Mancozeb
A contact protectant that does not stop the sheath blight fungus spreading inside the canopy. Money wasted here.
Thiram
A seed treatment. It does not stop sheath blight in the standing crop.
Chlorothalonil
A contact protectant that does not control sheath blight. Money wasted here.
Bordeaux mixture
Copper does not control the sheath blight fungus.
Copper oxychloride plus copper hydroxide
Copper does not control the sheath blight fungus.
prevent: Use the right seeding rate and avoid close spacing, so air and light reach the base of the hills.
Use a moderate nitrogen rate for the season and split it. Too much nitrogen feeds the disease.
Keep weeds down in the paddy and on the bunds, since many grasses carry the fungus.
Drain the field for a few days at maximum tillering to dry the base of the hills.
After harvest, plow deep so sick stubble goes under, and skim floating trash from the water at land preparation.
In corn, strip the lowest leaves and sheaths that touch the soil, and do not plant too dense.
bio: Trichoderma harzianum attacks the fungus. Where a Trichoderma product is sold, use it early, as field results are mixed.
Bacillus products give partial control when started at maximum tillering.
diseases.threshold: From maximum tillering, part 20 hills a week and look at the sheaths near the water. Spray only when lesions keep climbing the plant and spread from hill to hill in hot, humid weather, mostly from panicle initiation to booting, and aim at the lower sheaths.
diseases.rotate: The sheath blight fungus has learned to survive strobilurins (group 11) where they were sprayed alone, so far outside Asia. Use group 11 only in a mix, never twice in a row, and rotate with triazoles (3) or SDHIs (7).

diseases.name: Rice blast
diseases.local: Mata mata (Tagalog and Bisaya), agupaw (Waray), taya taya (Cebuano in Mindanao)
diseases.hint: Spindle or diamond shaped leaf spots with gray centers and reddish brown borders.

rice: Systemic and made for blast. It protects the neck when sprayed at early heading.
Tricyclazole works before infection: spray as panicles start to emerge, and again at half heading.
Blast in Japan and Vietnam already resists strobilurins. Use it at most once a crop, then rotate.
Fungi learn to survive this group quickly. Rotate it with tricyclazole or isoprothiolane.
Fungi learn to survive this group quickly. Rotate it with tricyclazole or isoprothiolane.
Blast in Japan and Vietnam already resists strobilurins. Use it at most once a crop, then rotate.
Blast in Japan and Vietnam already resists strobilurins. Use it at most once a crop, then rotate.
Isotianil wakes the plant's own defenses. Spray before the disease shows. Do not repeat group 11.
Contact only: it guards the leaf surface for a few days and does little against neck blast.
Contact only, and some blast in Vietnam has grown less sensitive to it. Weak on neck blast.
Weak on blast, and copper can scorch rice at heading. Keep it for bacterial problems.
A friendly bacterium with only mild effect on blast. It will not hold neck blast in wet weather.
Weak on blast, and copper can scorch rice at heading. Keep it for bacterial problems.
Weak on blast, and copper can scorch rice at heading. Keep it for bacterial problems.
A strobilurin used alone: blast in Asia has already learned to survive this group. A last resort.
A strobilurin used alone: blast in Asia has already learned to survive this group. A last resort.

prevent: Plant a blast resistant variety, and sow clean, healthy seed early, soon after the rains begin.
Split nitrogen into two or more doses and never pile it on.
Keep water on the field. Fields that dry out, above all rainfed ones, get much more blast.
Avoid close planting, and stay out of the crop while the leaves are wet.
On soils short of silicon, add calcium silicate or clean, blast free straw.
After a blast year, plow the stubble under at once, and rotate with mungo, corn or vegetables when you can.
bio: Bacillus and Trichoderma products give only mild help. Resistant seed and water do far more.
diseases.threshold: From tillering, check 20 hills a week for spindle shaped gray spots, more often after cool nights with long dew. Spray only when a susceptible variety meets wet, cloudy weather near heading, the field had neck blast before, or leaf blast showed at tillering: once as panicles start to emerge and again at about half heading.
diseases.rotate: Blast fungus in Japan and Vietnam already resists strobilurins (FRAC 11). Never spray group 11 alone or twice in a row. Rotate it with tricyclazole (16.1) or isoprothiolane (6), and pair it with a triazole (3).

diseases.name: Bacterial leaf blight
diseases.local: Nauga nga dahon and natala nga tanum (Cebuano), nadurot nga tanum (Waray), naggapula (Ilonggo), and kresek for the seedling wilt
diseases.hint: Yellow to orange stripes that start at the leaf tip or edge and move down with a wavy margin.
diseases.no: No spray cures it: the bacteria live inside the leaf veins, and copper only slows the spread a little.

rice: Only slows spread on the leaf surface. It cannot cure sick plants. Can scorch rice at flowering.
Only slows spread on the leaf surface. It cannot cure sick plants. Can scorch rice at flowering.
A copper made for rice bacterial diseases. It slows the spread when used early but cures nothing.
Only slows spread on the leaf surface. It cannot cure sick plants. Can scorch rice at flowering.
A friendly bacterium. Mild help at best, and only before the disease spreads.
Harsh on rice leaves and only slows the spread a little. A last resort.

avoid: Fosetyl aluminium
Made for water molds. It does not control this bacterium.
Streptomycin plus oxytetracycline
Medical antibiotics: farm use breeds bacteria that resist them, and the blight sits inside the leaf veins.
prevent: Plant a resistant variety, and change to another resistant variety if blight starts to break through.
Use clean seed from a healthy crop, and do not cut or bruise seedlings at pulling and transplanting.
Split nitrogen, never heavy, and keep potash enough. Lush, nitrogen rich rice is hit hardest.
Drain the field when blight shows, and keep water from a sick field from flowing into yours.
After harvest, plow under stubble, ratoons and volunteer rice, and keep grassy weeds off the bunds and canals.
Use wider spacing where blight is common, so leaves dry faster after rain.
bio: Bacillus products help a little as prevention. They do not cure a sick crop.
diseases.threshold: Scout from tillering, and right after storms, floods or strong winds, for wavy yellow stripes from the leaf tip or edge and milky drops on the leaf in the morning. At the first signs, act with water and fertilizer: drain the field, hold back nitrogen and add potash. Sprays will not turn it around.

diseases.name: Rice tungro
diseases.sci: Rice tungro bacilliform virus and rice tungro spherical virus
diseases.hint: Leaves that turn yellow or orange yellow, starting at the tip and spreading down the blade.
diseases.no: No spray cures tungro. Pull out sick hills, plant resistant varieties and plant together after a fallow.
avoid: Pymetrozine
A spray cannot cure tungro, and pymetrozine is weak on the green leafhopper. See the leafhopper's own list.
Buprofezin
Kills leafhopper nymphs only, not the winged adults that bring tungro in. It cannot cure the virus.
prevent: Plant a tungro resistant or leafhopper resistant variety where tungro has struck, and change varieties every few seasons.
Plant together across the barangay after a fallow, and avoid the weeks when leafhoppers peaked before.
Plow under stubble, ratoons and volunteer rice right after harvest. They carry the virus to the next crop.
Pull and bury sick hills early, and never take seedlings from a seedbed that shows yellow orange plants.
Do not plant next to a field that has tungro, and keep nitrogen at the right rate.
bio: Spiders, mirid bugs, dragonflies and damselflies eat green leafhoppers. Avoid early sprays so they stay.
diseases.threshold: Watch the seedbed and the first 40 days for hills that turn yellow to orange from the leaf tips, stay short and make few tillers, with green leafhoppers on them. Pull and bury sick hills at once. Once tungro is in the area a leafhopper spray rarely stops it, so ask a technician before you spray.

diseases.name: Brown spot of rice
diseases.hint: Small, circular, dark brown to purple brown spots on the leaves from tillering on.

rice: Spray only if the spots keep coming after you fix the seed and soil. Do not use group 11 twice in a row.
A contact protectant: it guards new leaves and the panicle but cannot heal spots already there.
A contact protectant: it guards new leaves and the panicle but cannot heal spots already there.
A contact protectant: it guards new leaves and the panicle but cannot heal spots already there.
Weak on the brown spot fungus. A triazole mix or a protectant does better.

prevent: Use clean seed, or treat your own seed in hot water at 53 to 54 degrees Celsius for 10 to 12 minutes, after an 8 hour cold soak.
Test the soil and give what it lacks, above all potash, and silicon on poor soils.
Keep water on the field where you can. Brown spot is worst in dry, unflooded soil.
Remove volunteer rice, crop debris and weeds that carry the fungus between seasons.
Plant a resistant variety, above all in direct seeded or rainfed fields.
bio: Seed treated with Trichoderma, where sold, gives seedlings a cleaner start.
diseases.threshold: Brown spot is a sign of hungry or dry soil more than a reason to spray. Check 20 hills from tillering. Spray only if spots keep spreading to the upper leaves and the flag leaf after you fix the soil, or the field had spotted grain before, at booting to heading.

diseases.name: False smut
diseases.hint: A few grains on a panicle swell into balls that are over twice the size of a normal grain.
prevent: Use clean, certified seed. If unsure, treat it in hot water at 52 degrees Celsius for 10 minutes before sowing.
Keep nitrogen moderate and split it. Heavy nitrogen before heading invites the fungus.
Avoid close planting, and alternate flooding and drying where you can, to cut humidity in the crop.
Pick smut balls as soon as you see them, before they turn green black, and carry them out in a bag.
After harvest, remove or plow under straw and stubble, and time planting so flowering misses the rainiest weeks.
diseases.threshold: You cannot wait for the balls to decide: by then a spray is too late. Decide at late booting: spray only in a field that had false smut before, when humid, cloudy or rainy weather is forecast for flowering.

diseases.name: Bacterial leaf streak
diseases.hint: Narrow, water soaked streaks run between the veins of the leaf, with straight sides.
diseases.no: No product cures it. Clean seed, resistant varieties and drainage keep it out. Copper only slows it a little.

rice: Only slows spread on the leaf surface after draining. It cures nothing. Can scorch rice at flowering.
Only slows spread on the leaf surface after draining. It cures nothing. Can scorch rice at flowering.
Only slows spread on the leaf surface after draining. It cures nothing. Can scorch rice at flowering.

prevent: Sow certified seed of a variety that has held up in your area, and never save seed from a field that had streak.
Pull out grassy weeds around the field and in the bunds. The bacterium lives on them between crops.
Split nitrogen into small doses and add potash in splits, so leaves stay firm and harder to wound.
Drain the field when streak shows, and do not let water from sick fields flow into healthy ones.
After harvest, plow under or remove the stubble, and rotate with another crop when you can.
diseases.threshold: Scout during tillering in wet, windy weeks for narrow, water soaked streaks between the veins that turn yellow with tiny amber drops. At the first streaks, drain the field and hold back nitrogen. A copper spray comes only after that, and only if the streaks keep spreading.

diseases.name: Sheath rot
diseases.hint: Oblong or irregular spots form on the top leaf sheath, with dark reddish brown edges and gray centers.

rice: Spray at booting where sheath rot was bad before. Once the panicle is stuck, a spray cannot free it.
A protectant with only mild effect on sheath rot, and copper can scorch the emerging panicle.

prevent: Use healthy seed from a field free of the disease, and treat the seed before sowing if the field had sheath rot.
Do not plant too close. Sheath rot rises with planting density.
Split the nitrogen and add potash instead of more nitrogen.
Control stem borers and sheath mites, whose wounds let the fungus in, but keep insecticides off for the first 30 to 40 days.
Remove infected stubble and crop residue after harvest, and plow it under.
diseases.threshold: From booting, check the flag leaf sheath on 20 hills for oblong spots with gray centers and brown edges, and for panicles that fail to come out. Spray at booting only in fields with a history of sheath rot. After the panicle is trapped it is too late.

diseases.name: Narrow brown leaf spot
diseases.hint: Thin, straight brown lines run parallel to the veins on the leaf and the upper sheath.

rice: Rarely needed: the disease is usually minor. Spray only a susceptible variety at panicle initiation or early boot.
Rarely needed: the disease is usually minor. Spray only a susceptible variety at panicle initiation or early boot.
Rarely needed. Fungi learn to survive this group quickly, so use it once and rotate.
Weak on this leaf spot, and copper can scorch rice at heading.

prevent: Test the soil and fix a potassium shortage with potash. The disease follows potassium poor soils.
Use certified seed of a variety that shows less of the disease.
Follow the recommended nitrogen rate, or the leaf color chart, so you do not overfeed.
Keep weeds down in the field and on the bunds, and add organic matter to build the soil.
Plant at the best time for your area, and clear diseased straw and stubble after harvest.
diseases.threshold: Usually minor. Check the upper leaves and sheaths from panicle initiation. A spray pays only on a susceptible variety when thin brown streaks spread onto the flag leaf before heading.

diseases.name: Rice grassy stunt
diseases.hint: Plants are severely stunted, with many thin tillers and a grassy, rosette look.
diseases.no: No spray cures the virus. Fight the brown planthopper that carries it, with resistant seed and planting together first.
prevent: Plant a variety that resists the brown planthopper, or the virus, or both.
Plant together with the farms around you and keep a fallow, so hoppers cannot move from old fields onto young ones.
Pull out and bury sick plants early, and plow under stubble, ratoons and volunteer rice after harvest.
Flood the seedbed for a day when planthoppers are on it, so they drown.
No insecticide in the first 30 to 40 days, and never a pyrethroid: both bring planthoppers back worse.
Avoid close planting, and leave a narrow walking gap every few meters to scout.
bio: Spiders, mirid bugs, water striders and egg wasps keep planthoppers in check. Spare them by not spraying early.
diseases.threshold: Where grassy stunt showed before, tap 20 hills a week for brown planthoppers from the seedbed through tillering, and look for stunted hills with many thin, upright, pale tillers. The virus spreads at hopper counts far below hopperburn, so pull sick hills at once and use only the selective hopper sprays when counts climb.

diseases.name: Rice ragged stunt
diseases.hint: Plants are severely stunted in the early growth stages, with short, dark green leaves.
diseases.no: No spray cures the virus. Fight the brown planthopper that carries it, with resistant seed and planting together first.
prevent: Plant a resistant variety: some resist the planthopper, some the virus, some both.
Plant at the same time as the farms around you, and leave a fallow or rotate so volunteer rice does not keep the virus.
Pull out and bury sick plants early, and destroy infected stubble and crop residue after harvest.
Flood the seedbed for a day when planthoppers are on it, so they drown.
No insecticide in the first 30 to 40 days, and never a pyrethroid: both bring planthoppers back worse.
bio: Spiders, mirid bugs and egg wasps eat planthoppers. Spare them by not spraying early.
diseases.threshold: Where ragged stunt showed before, tap 20 hills a week for brown planthoppers from the seedbed through tillering, and look for short, dark green hills with ragged, twisted leaf edges. The virus spreads at hopper counts far below hopperburn, so pull sick hills at once and use only the selective hopper sprays when counts climb.

diseases.name: Bakanae
diseases.hint: Seedlings several inches taller than their neighbors, thin and arching over the healthy plants.
diseases.no: A spray on the standing crop does not help. Treat the seed before sowing and pull the sick plants.
prevent: Buy certified, clean seed, and never save seed from a field that had tall, pale plants.
Float the seed in salt water or plain water and throw away the light seeds that float.
Soak seed you trust in hot water at 55 to 57 degrees Celsius before sowing. It fails on heavily infected seed.
Pull the tall seedlings out of the seedbed and the field, and bury them away from the paddy.
Plow in the straw and stubble right after harvest, and rotate away from rice for two years after a bad outbreak.
bio: Seed treated with Trichoderma, where sold, lowers bakanae a little.
diseases.threshold: Check the seedbed and the young field every week for seedlings taller, thinner and paler than the rest. Pull and bury them at once, before they shed spores at flowering. A few sick plants in a hundred is reason to change the seed source next season.
diseases.rotate: Bakanae fungus in China, Japan and Korea has resisted benzimidazoles (carbendazim, thiophanate methyl) after long seed treatment use. Pair them with thiram or captan, and switch seed source when bakanae keeps coming back.

diseases.name: Rice stem rot
diseases.hint: Small, irregular black spots on the outer leaf sheath at the waterline.

rice: A contact protectant with little effect on stem rot at the waterline. Drainage, potash and stubble removal do more.

prevent: Destroy the hard black resting bodies after harvest: plow straw and stubble deep, or remove them, and let the field dry.
Balance the fertilizer: too much nitrogen with too little potassium raises stem rot. Split doses of potash lower it.
Drain the field now and then during the crop, since floodwater carries the floating resting bodies.
Control stem borers and planthoppers that wound the stem, but keep sprays off for the first 30 to 40 days.
Rotate with a legume or forage crop when you can, since no variety is highly resistant.
diseases.threshold: From late tillering, part 20 hills and look at the outer sheath at the waterline for small black spots that grow and darken the stem. A spray seldom pays. In a field with a clear history of stem rot, act at the first lesions with drainage and potash, and spray only on a technician's advice.

diseases.name: Corn downy mildew
diseases.hint: Pale or yellow stripes on the first true leaves of young seedlings.

corn_yellow: A seed treatment of group 40: the partner for fields where metalaxyl no longer holds the mildew.
A spray that shields young plants from the spores of sick neighbors. It does not cure striped plants.
A seed treatment. This mildew has grown resistant to metalaxyl in parts of Asia, so pair or rotate it with dimethomorph.
A seed treatment. This mildew has grown resistant to metalaxyl in parts of Asia, so pair or rotate it with dimethomorph.
corn_sweet: A seed treatment of group 40: the partner for fields where metalaxyl no longer holds the mildew.
A spray that shields young plants from the spores of sick neighbors. It does not cure striped plants.
A seed treatment. This mildew has grown resistant to metalaxyl in parts of Asia, so pair or rotate it with dimethomorph.
A seed treatment. This mildew has grown resistant to metalaxyl in parts of Asia, so pair or rotate it with dimethomorph.
corn_glutinous: A seed treatment of group 40: the partner for fields where metalaxyl no longer holds the mildew.
A spray that shields young plants from the spores of sick neighbors. It does not cure striped plants.
A seed treatment. This mildew has grown resistant to metalaxyl in parts of Asia, so pair or rotate it with dimethomorph.
A seed treatment. This mildew has grown resistant to metalaxyl in parts of Asia, so pair or rotate it with dimethomorph.

avoid: Chlorothalonil
A contact spray cannot reach downy mildew inside the plant. Seed treatment and pulling sick plants do the work.
prevent: Plant treated seed of a resistant or tolerant hybrid. Resistance is the main defense.
Plant on time with your neighbors, so young corn never stands beside older infected corn or sugarcane.
Pull, bag and burn striped seedlings in the first three weeks, before they shed spores.
Clear volunteer corn, sorghum and wild grasses such as talahib from the field and its edges.
Drain the field well and avoid planting where water stands.
diseases.threshold: From emergence to about day 30, walk the field early in the morning, when white down shows under striped leaves. A striped seedling never yields, so pull and destroy every one at once. If many seedlings stripe in the first two weeks, the seed treatment failed and the next planting needs another group.
diseases.rotate: This mildew has lost sensitivity to metalaxyl (group 4) seed treatment in parts of Asia. Where metalaxyl has failed, switch to a dimethomorph (group 40) seed treatment or use the two together, and never rely on metalaxyl alone season after season.

diseases.name: Corn rust
diseases.hint: Small, round to oval pustules on the leaves, brown, orange or brick red.

corn_yellow: Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
A protectant: it only works when sprayed before the pustules spread.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
corn_sweet: Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
A protectant: it only works when sprayed before the pustules spread.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
corn_glutinous: Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
A protectant: it only works when sprayed before the pustules spread.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.

prevent: Plant a resistant hybrid: it is the best and cheapest rust control.
Plant early or in the drier season, and do not plant beside an older infected field.
Destroy volunteer corn, and plow under or remove the crop residue after harvest.
Remove Oxalis weeds near the field, since they can host common rust.
Feed balanced nitrogen with enough potassium.
diseases.threshold: From the 8 leaf stage to dough, check the ear leaf and the leaves above it on 20 plants at each of five spots every week. A spray rarely pays on field corn. On sweet corn or a susceptible hybrid in wet weather, start at about six pustules per leaf on the ear leaf or above, before the dough stage.

diseases.name: Northern corn leaf blight
diseases.hint: Long, narrow tan lesions along the leaf edge on the lower leaves, the first sign.

corn_yellow: A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
corn_sweet: A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
corn_glutinous: A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.

prevent: Plant a resistant hybrid. Most good hybrids carry resistance, and it beats any spray.
Plow under or remove corn residue after harvest, since the fungus lives on it for up to two years.
Rotate with a crop that is not a grass, and clear volunteer corn, sorghum and grassy weeds.
Feed enough phosphorus and potassium, and do not oversupply nitrogen.
Keep to the right spacing, so the canopy dries quickly after rain.
diseases.threshold: From about the 14 leaf stage to tasseling, check the leaves below the ear on 20 plants at each of five spots every week. Spray only a susceptible hybrid in wet weather, when lesions reach the ear leaf or above at tasseling. A spray at tasseling to early silking has the best chance to pay.

diseases.name: Banded leaf and sheath blight
diseases.hint: Water soaked, discolored bands and rings on the leaf sheaths, brown, tan or gray.

corn_yellow: Aim it at the lower sheaths as soon as the first bands show.
Aim it at the lower stalk and sheaths at the first bands. Group 11, so alternate with a group 3 product.
Group 11 like azoxystrobin: do not rotate the two with each other.
corn_sweet: Aim it at the lower sheaths as soon as the first bands show.
Aim it at the lower stalk and sheaths at the first bands. Group 11, so alternate with a group 3 product.
Group 11 like azoxystrobin: do not rotate the two with each other.
corn_glutinous: Aim it at the lower sheaths as soon as the first bands show.
Aim it at the lower stalk and sheaths at the first bands. Group 11, so alternate with a group 3 product.
Group 11 like azoxystrobin: do not rotate the two with each other.

prevent: Strip the two or three lowest leaves with their sheaths at about day 40. It slows the fungus as it climbs.
Use wider spacing and avoid dense stands that hold humidity.
Do not plant corn right after rice that had sheath blight, and keep water from a sick field away from a clean one.
Clear grass weeds, and bury or burn crop debris after harvest.
Plant a tolerant hybrid where one is sold.
bio: Trichoderma or Bacillus subtilis on the seed and soil slow the fungus. Use them before chemical sprays.
diseases.threshold: From about day 30 to tasseling, check the lower sheaths of 20 plants at each of five spots every week, and more often after warm rains. Act at the first water soaked bands on the lower sheaths, before they climb to the ear. Once the ear rots, a spray comes too late.

diseases.name: Corn stalk rot
diseases.sci: Fusarium spp., Pythium aphanidermatum, Dickeya zeae
diseases.hint: Plants that wilt or turn gray and brown while the grain is filling.
diseases.no: No spray stops stalk rot: balanced feeding with enough potassium, the right spacing, good drainage and borer control prevent it.
prevent: Balance nitrogen with enough potassium, given in split doses: high nitrogen with low potassium invites stalk rot.
Do not overcrowd. Keep to the spacing on the seed bag.
Control the corn borer, whose tunnels let the rot into the stalk.
Drain the field and avoid water standing around the stalks. The bacterial form spreads in water.
Choose hybrids with strong stalks, and harvest the weakest fields first.
Rotate with a crop that is not a grass, and plow under the residue.
diseases.threshold: From dent stage, pinch the lowest stalk joint or push sideways on 20 plants at each of five spots. When more than 1 stalk in 10 crushes or bends, harvest that field first, before it lodges.

diseases.name: Corn ear rot
diseases.hint: Pinkish white, cottony or powdery growth on the cob and between kernels, the sign of Fusarium.

corn_yellow: Sprayed at silking it only partly lowers ear rot. It cannot clean ears that are already moldy.
Strobilurins are weak on Fusarium ear rot. A group 3 spray at silking does more.
A protectant labeled for Diplodia rot. It does little once the fungi are inside the husk.
corn_sweet: Sprayed at silking it only partly lowers ear rot. It cannot clean ears that are already moldy.
Strobilurins are weak on Fusarium ear rot. A group 3 spray at silking does more.
A protectant labeled for Diplodia rot. It does little once the fungi are inside the husk.
corn_glutinous: Sprayed at silking it only partly lowers ear rot. It cannot clean ears that are already moldy.
Strobilurins are weak on Fusarium ear rot. A group 3 spray at silking does more.
A protectant labeled for Diplodia rot. It does little once the fungi are inside the husk.

avoid: Copper sulfate
Copper does not stop the Fusarium and Aspergillus fungi that rot ears.
prevent: Control earworm and corn borer, whose holes let the ear rot fungi in.
Plant tolerant hybrids with tight husks that cover the ear tip.
Avoid drought stress and nitrogen shortage at flowering. Aspergillus hits stressed corn hardest.
Harvest on time, and dry the grain to 13 to 15 percent moisture within about two days.
Sort out moldy ears before storage, and clean the store and the sheller first.
Rotate away from corn, and bury or remove the residue that carries the fungi.
diseases.threshold: At silking and again before harvest, peel back the husks of 20 ears at each of five spots. A spray seldom pays. When you find mold or insect damaged ears, harvest as soon as the grain is mature, keep moldy ears apart and dry the rest to 13 to 15 percent within about two days.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.hint: Sudden wilting of the whole plant while the leaves are still green.
diseases.no: No spray works. The bacteria live inside the water vessels of the stem, out of reach. Graft, rotate and plant resistant varieties.
avoid: Copper sulfate
Copper cannot reach bacteria that live inside the stem. It will not stop bacterial wilt, whatever the label says.
prevent: Graft tomato, eggplant or pepper onto a resistant rootstock, or plant a resistant variety. This is the surest answer in fields with a wilt history.
Raise seedlings in clean, sterilized media, and plant only healthy seed tubers and ginger rhizomes from fields free of wilt.
Rotate for three to four years with rice, corn or other grasses. Flooded rice in between helps clear the soil.
Plant on raised beds, drain the field well, and never let water run from a sick field into a clean one.
Pull wilted plants with the soil around the roots and destroy them away from the field. Wash tools and boots before entering a clean field.
Avoid cutting roots when weeding, and keep root knot nematodes down, since their wounds let the bacteria in.
bio: Compost and other organic matter feed soil microbes that compete with the bacteria. They help, but they do not replace grafting and rotation.
diseases.threshold: Cut a wilted stem near the soil and hang it in a glass of clear water. A milky stream oozing out within minutes confirms bacterial wilt. Pull every wilted plant at once. No level of disease makes a spray pay.

diseases.name: Damping off
diseases.sci: Pythium spp., Rhizoctonia solani, Fusarium spp.
diseases.hint: Gaps in the seedbed because seeds rotted before they sprouted.

cotton: For seed and seedbed treatment only. It does little against Pythium once roots rot.
celery: Best as a seed treatment or a seedbed drench at sowing. Young seedlings are tender, so follow the label closely.
tomato: Use it on the seed or as a drench at sowing. It guards healthy seedlings but cannot save ones already falling over.
Protects the stem base from Rhizoctonia and leaf infections. Weak against Pythium root rot.
chili: Use it on the seed or as a drench at sowing. It guards healthy seedlings but cannot save ones already falling over.
bellpepper: Use it on the seed or as a drench at sowing. It guards healthy seedlings but cannot save ones already falling over.
watermelon: Use it on the seed or as a drench at sowing. It guards healthy seedlings but cannot save ones already falling over.
Works best on Rhizoctonia. For Pythium rot in waterlogged trays it is not enough on its own.

prevent: Heat or steam the seedbed soil or tray mix before sowing, or use a clean soilless mix such as coir with compost.
Use clean trays and tools, and water with clean rainwater or tap water, not pond or ditch water.
Sow thin and shallow in raised, well drained beds, and water only enough to keep the mix moist.
Give the seedbed sun and moving air, and never stack filled trays or crowd the seedlings.
Use treated or healthy seed, and keep fresh manure out of the seedbed.
Remove sick seedlings with the soil around them at once.
bio: Coat the seed with Trichoderma or mix it into the tray media before sowing. It guards roots against Pythium, Rhizoctonia and Fusarium.
Bacillus based products used as a seed soak or drench add protection at sowing.
diseases.threshold: Count gaps and fallen seedlings in the seedbed every morning for the first two weeks after sowing. Act at the first patch of collapsed seedlings: lift them out with the soil around them, water less, and drench the rest with a registered product.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.sci: Alternaria solani (on tomato also named Alternaria linariae)
diseases.hint: Small brown spots with yellow edges appear first on the oldest, lowest leaves.

potato: Copper is weaker on early blight than mancozeb or chlorothalonil. It earns its place when bacterial spot is also in the field.
Weaker on early blight than mancozeb or chlorothalonil. Keep it as a rotation partner, not the main spray.
tomato: Early blight has grown resistant to strobilurins in many countries: use it only beside a protectant and never twice in a row.
A biological: start before the spots spread. It holds light early blight, not a bad outbreak.
Copper is weaker on early blight than mancozeb or chlorothalonil. It earns its place when bacterial spot is also in the field.
Copper is weaker on early blight than mancozeb or chlorothalonil, and a strong mix can scorch young tomato leaves.
Weaker on early blight than mancozeb or chlorothalonil. Keep it as a rotation partner, not the main spray.
Copper is weaker on early blight than mancozeb or chlorothalonil. It earns its place when bacterial spot is also in the field.
Copper is weaker on early blight than mancozeb or chlorothalonil. It earns its place when bacterial spot is also in the field.

avoid: Mancozeb plus metalaxyl
Metalaxyl does nothing to early blight and wastes a late blight tool. Buy plain mancozeb for early blight.
prevent: Start with clean seed and healthy seedlings, and throw out any seedling with dark leaf spots or a sunken lesion on the stem.
Stake or trellis tomato and prune the lowest leaves so the canopy dries fast after rain.
Mulch the beds so rain does not splash soil and spores onto the lower leaves.
Feed the crop well through the season. Hungry plants carrying a heavy fruit load get the worst early blight.
Rotate for two or three years away from tomato, potato, eggplant and pepper, and plow under or remove crop debris after harvest.
Water at the base early in the day, not over the leaves late in the afternoon.
bio: Bacillus based biofungicides can hold light early blight when sprayed before the spots climb the plant.
diseases.threshold: Check the lowest leaves twice a week from the first flowers. Start protectant sprays when the first target spots show on the lower leaves in warm, wet weather, or from transplanting in fields that had the disease before.
diseases.rotate: Early blight has become resistant to the strobilurins (FRAC 11) and to some SDHI fungicides (FRAC 7) in many countries. Use them only in mixes or in turn with mancozeb or chlorothalonil, never more than two sprays of one group in a row.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.hint: Brown or black patches start at the leaf tips and edges and spread fast across the veins.

potato: A protectant: it must coat the leaf before the spores land, and heavy rain washes it off, so spray again after a downpour.
A protectant: it must coat the leaf before the spores land. Keep it in every spray as the partner of the systemic products.
Only the azoxystrobin part acts on late blight. Pick it when early blight is in the field too, and never twice in a row.
A protectant that works well on late blight. It does not move into the leaf, so spray before infection.
Better on root and stem rot water molds than on leaves. On late blight use it in a mix or beside a protectant.
Late blight resists metalaxyl in many places: use it only early, before spots show, and no more than two or three times a season.
Made for early blight and leaf spots. It is weak on late blight, so keep a true water mold spray in the program.
Weak on late blight. It is a fair protectant for other leaf diseases but should not be the main late blight spray.
Late blight resists metalaxyl in many places: use it only early, before spots show, and no more than two or three times a season.
Mostly a seed and soil fungicide. On late blight leaves it protects less well than mancozeb.
A biological: it helps only when disease pressure is low and cannot hold late blight in cool, wet weather.
Same group as metalaxyl, so the same resistance: use it only early, before spots show, and only a few times a season.
tomato: A protectant: it must coat the leaf before the spores land, and heavy rain washes it off, so spray again after a downpour.
A protectant: it must coat the leaf before the spores land. Keep it in every spray as the partner of the systemic products.
Weaker on late blight than the water mold sprays: mix it with a protectant and never use it twice in a row.
Better on root and stem rot water molds than on leaves. On late blight use it in a mix or beside a protectant.
Only the azoxystrobin part acts on late blight. Pick it when early blight is in the field too, and never twice in a row.
Late blight resists metalaxyl in many places: use it only early, before spots show, and no more than two or three times a season.
Weak on late blight. It is a fair protectant for other leaf diseases but should not be the main late blight spray.
Late blight resists metalaxyl in many places: use it only early, before spots show, and no more than two or three times a season.

prevent: Plant certified clean seed tubers and healthy tomato seedlings. One sick tuber can start the disease in a whole field.
Grow a resistant or tolerant variety where one suits your area. It cuts the number of sprays a season needs.
Plant on ridges with good drainage and enough room between rows so the leaves dry quickly after rain and fog.
Hill up potato rows well so spores washed off the leaves do not reach the tubers. Kill blighted vines about two weeks before digging.
Destroy cull piles and volunteer potato and tomato plants, and do not plant a new crop beside an older infected one.
Water at the base of the plants, not over the leaves, and do not overfeed with nitrogen.
bio: Bacillus biofungicides give a little help under light pressure, but no biological holds late blight on its own in the wet season.
diseases.threshold: In cool, misty weather walk the field every two or three days and turn the lower and middle leaves. On susceptible varieties start protectant sprays before the first spots when cool nights and wet mornings set in. At the first spots switch to a systemic water mold spray within a day or two and keep the interval short while the weather stays wet.
diseases.rotate: Late blight resists metalaxyl and the other phenylamides (FRAC 4) in many places in Asia, so never use them alone or as a cure. Turn the systemic groups each spray (27, 40, 21, 43, 45, 49) and keep mancozeb or chlorothalonil in every tank.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.sci: Podosphaera xanthii, Erysiphe spp., Leveillula taurica
diseases.hint: Round white spots, like flour, appear on the leaves, the leaf stalks and the stems.

mungbean: Spray in the cool morning or evening, never in midday heat or within two weeks of an oil spray. Some melon types scorch from it.
Cucurbit powdery mildew resists benomyl and its kin almost everywhere. On legumes and papaya change group after one or two sprays.
Works on bean and mungbean mildew, but this group wears out fast: spray at the first spots and change group after one or two sprays.
Cucurbit powdery mildew resists this group almost everywhere. On legumes, papaya and strawberry change group after one or two sprays.
wingedbean: Spray in the cool morning or evening, never in midday heat or within two weeks of an oil spray. Some melon types scorch from it.
limabean: Spray in the cool morning or evening, never in midday heat or within two weeks of an oil spray. Some melon types scorch from it.
pechay: Spray in the cool morning or evening, never in midday heat or within two weeks of an oil spray. Some melon types scorch from it.
A contact protectant: it slows the mildew on the upper leaf but misses the underside. Pair it with a product that moves into the leaf.
ampalaya: Strong on powdery mildew, but both parts can wear out: use it at most twice a season and turn to sulfur or a triazole between.

avoid: Mancozeb
Mancozeb does little against powdery mildew. Use sulfur or a triazole for it instead.
Azoxystrobin
Cucurbit powdery mildew resists strobilurins widely in Asia. Azoxystrobin alone often fails on it.
prevent: Plant a tolerant or resistant variety where one is sold. Good types exist for cucumber, melon, squash and ampalaya.
Choose a sunny, airy spot and do not crowd the plants. Shade and still, humid air speed the mildew up.
Clear weeds in and around the field, and do not plant beside an older crop that already shows white spots.
Pick off the first spotted leaves, and plow under or remove old vines and plants right after the last harvest.
Avoid too much nitrogen, which grows soft, lush leaves that the mildew loves.
bio: Small yellow and black ladybirds (Illeis) graze on the white mildew. Broad insecticide sprays kill them.
Potassium bicarbonate, plant oils and Bacillus based products work as early protectants for organic growers, best before the spots spread.
diseases.threshold: From the first flowers, turn 50 older leaves across the field and look at both sides. Start spraying when one leaf in 50 shows white spots. Waiting until the leaves turn white loses the crop.
diseases.rotate: Cucurbit powdery mildew resists the benomyl group (FRAC 1) and the strobilurins (FRAC 11) widely in Asia, and the triazoles (FRAC 3) slowly lose strength. Turn sulfur or chlorothalonil with a triazole or an SDHI (FRAC 7) mix, and never spray one group twice in a row.

prevent: Plant a tolerant or resistant variety. In the rainy season it is the cheapest protection you can buy.
Water early in the day at the base of the vines so the leaves dry before night.
Space the plants well, run rows with the usual wind, and keep the trellis open so the leaves dry fast.
Pick off infected older leaves early, pull badly sick vines, and plow under old vines right after the last harvest.
Do not plant a new crop beside an old infected one, and avoid the wettest weeks of the year when you can.
diseases.threshold: From the first runners, check the older leaves twice a week, more often after rainy nights and heavy dew. Start protectant sprays when the wet weather sets in, and move to a product made for downy mildew at the first yellow angular spots.
diseases.rotate: Cucurbit downy mildew resists the strobilurins (FRAC 11) and metalaxyl (FRAC 4) widely in Asia, and resistance to the CAA group (FRAC 40) has been found in some countries. Keep mancozeb or chlorothalonil in every spray and change the downy mildew group (21, 28 with 43, 40) each time.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.hint: Plants droop even though the soil is still wet.

cabbage: Use it as a soil drench at or just after transplanting. It protects young roots but cannot cure roots already clubbed.
A biological: it gives partial control at best. Use it with lime and clean seedlings, never alone.

prevent: Lime the field to a pH of 7.1 to 7.5 before transplanting. Test the soil first so you lime enough.
Raise seedlings in clean trays with pasteurized or soilless mix, and never buy seedlings from a field with clubroot.
Plant on raised beds and open the drains. Wet soil lets the spores swim to the roots.
Grow a clubroot resistant cabbage or Chinese cabbage variety in fields with a history of the disease.
Wash soil off boots, tools and tillers before moving from an infested field to a clean one.
Rotate away from the cabbage family for as long as you can and pull cabbage family weeds. The spores live many years.
bio: In trials, lime plus the soil fungus Paecilomyces lilacinus gave better control than lime alone.
Bacillus based soil products add a little protection when used with lime.
diseases.threshold: Dig up a few plants that wilt at midday and recover at night. Swollen, club shaped roots confirm it. There is no spray threshold: once roots are clubbed, plan lime, clean seedlings and a soil treatment for the next crop.

diseases.name: Black rot of cabbage
diseases.hint: Yellow to brown V shaped patches start at the leaf edge.

cabbage: Copper only slows the spread in the nursery and young field in wet weather. It cannot cure a plant with black veins.
