prevent: Buy certified clean seed, and never save seed from a crop that had black rot. The bacterium lives in seed for years.
Soak doubtful cabbage seed in hot water at 50 degrees Celsius for 25 minutes. It lowers the risk but can lower germination.
Raise seedlings in clean trays, clean tools with diluted bleach, and discard any seedling with a spot.
Rotate for two to three years away from the cabbage family, pull cabbage family weeds, and plow under crop debris right after harvest.
Avoid overhead watering, and stay out of the field while the leaves are wet.
Keep diamondback moth and other caterpillars down, since their feeding wounds let the bacteria in.
bio: Protect the small wasps and spiders that hold diamondback moth down. Fewer caterpillar wounds mean fewer ways in for the bacteria.
diseases.threshold: From the seedbed on, check the leaf edges every week for yellow V shaped patches with black veins inside. Throw out any spotted seedling before transplanting. In the field, a copper spray pays only when the first plants show it early in a rainy spell.

diseases.name: Bacterial soft rot
diseases.hint: Water soaked spots appear on outer leaves, stems, heads or fruit, then grow and sink.
diseases.no: No spray stops soft rot. The bacteria enter through wounds and wet tissue, so drain the field, handle gently and keep chewing pests down.
prevent: Plant on raised, well drained beds, and give plants room so the leaves dry fast after rain.
Water by drip or furrow, not over the leaves, and mulch to stop soil splashing onto the plants.
Keep diamondback moth, cutworms and other chewing pests down, and handle plants gently. Every wound lets the bacteria in.
Harvest in dry weather, avoid bruising, and cure onion, potato and ginger before storing them cool, dry and airy.
Pull and destroy sick plants at once, never compost them, and clean knives between plants with bleach or alcohol.
Rotate with grains such as corn or rice, and do not overfeed with nitrogen, which makes soft, easily rotted tissue.
diseases.threshold: Check heads, stems, bulbs and stored produce for soft, water soaked, foul smelling rot, most after heavy rain or a hot, wet harvest. Remove every rotting plant or tuber at once. There is no spray threshold.

diseases.name: Tomato leaf curl
diseases.hint: The leaf edges curl upward and inward, and the leaflets are small and puckered.
diseases.no: No spray cures the virus. Raise seedlings under net, pull sick plants early, keep whiteflies down and plant resistant varieties.
prevent: Raise seedlings under fine insect net, and plant only seedlings free of whiteflies and curled leaves.
Plant a tolerant or resistant tomato variety where one is sold. It is the surest protection in whitefly seasons.
Pull the first curled plants early, bag them before carrying them out, and destroy the crop residue after harvest.
Leave a few weeks with no tomato or pepper in the area between crops, and do not plant beside an older infected field.
Keep borders free of weeds that host whitefly, and use yellow sticky traps and silver reflective mulch to keep whiteflies off.
Plant a few rows of corn or sorghum around the field as a barrier against whiteflies blowing in.
bio: Small parasitic wasps, lacewings and ladybirds feed on whiteflies. Do not spray borders and weeds with broad insecticides.
Beauveria or Metarhizium sprays on the leaf underside lower whitefly numbers. They do not stop the virus in a plant already sick.
diseases.threshold: In the nursery any whitefly is too many: keep seedlings under net. In the field, check the underside of 20 top leaves twice a week for the first six weeks and act on whiteflies early, since plants infected in the first month lose the most fruit.

avoid: Potassium silicate
A plant tonic, not a fungicide: it does not stop the anthracnose fungus.
prevent: Mango: induce flowering for a dry stretch if you can. Flowers that open in steady rain are where anthracnose starts.
Bag mango fruit with paper bags at 55 to 60 days after flower induction, and dip the harvest 10 minutes in water at 53 degrees Celsius.
Prune dead twigs and dried mummy fruit, rake up fallen leaves and rotten fruit, and carry them out. The next spores live there.
Prune the canopy open after harvest so flowers and leaves dry fast after rain, and keep trees low enough to spray and bag.
Sili and beans: plant clean seed, never seed from spotted pods, rotate away from pepper and tomato, and water at the base.
Handle fruit gently and keep fruit flies and thrips down. Every bruise or sting opens a door for the fungus.
bio: Bacillus based biologicals can stand in for a protectant in dry weeks, but they do not hold anthracnose in steady rain.
Trichoderma is being tried against onion twister. It is not yet a proven field control.
diseases.threshold: Mango: from bud break, check the flower clusters twice a week and protect them before rain or heavy dew. Blackened, dried flowers mean infection has already begun. Sili, beans and melons: act at the first sunken spots on pods or fruit when wet weather goes on.
diseases.rotate: Anthracnose fungi in Asian mango orchards often resist group 1 (benomyl, carbendazim, thiophanate methyl), and group 11 (strobilurins) loses ground fast when used alone. Build the season on mancozeb or chlorothalonil, slot in prochloraz or a group 3 plus 11 mix in the wettest weeks, and never spray one systemic group twice in a row.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.hint: Older leaves yellow and wilt, with brown streaks inside the stem.
diseases.no: No fungicide cures it or cleans the soil. Keep it out with clean planting material, plant resistant varieties and isolate sick plants at once.

banana: A soil biological that may slow new infection at planting. It cannot save a plant that already wilts.
A soil drench that may hold the fungus back around young roots. It does not cure a sick plant or clean the soil.
tomato: A soil biological that may slow new infection at planting. It cannot save a plant that already wilts.
watermelon: A soil biological that may slow new infection at planting. It cannot save a plant that already wilts.

avoid: Isotianil
Only wakes the plant's own defense. No proof it stops the wilt, so spend on clean plantlets and quarantine.
Thiophanate methyl
Its banana label is for diamond fruit spot, not the wilt. No fungicide cures fusarium wilt.
Fosetyl aluminium plus isotianil
Only wakes the plant's own defense. No proof it stops the wilt, so spend on clean plantlets and quarantine.
Azoxystrobin plus mancozeb
A leaf spray cannot reach a wilt fungus inside the stem. It will not save wilting tomato.
prevent: Plant clean tissue culture plantlets from an accredited nursery. Never take suckers from a sick mat or from another farm.
Where TR4 is near, plant resistant Cavendish selections or tolerant types, and never replant a susceptible banana where a sick one stood.
Scrape mud off boots, tools and tires before they enter, then dip them. Change the foot bath often because soil weakens it.
Kill a sick banana where it stands with herbicide, let it dry in place, fence the spot and keep its runoff away from clean blocks.
Tomato, melons and onions: rotate out of the same crop family for years, lime acid soil, and use grafted or resistant seedlings on old wilt ground.
Avoid cutting roots with deep cultivation and keep nematodes down. Root wounds let the fungus in.
bio: Trichoderma or Bacillus products worked into the planting hole may slow new infections. They do not cure a sick plant.
Compost and cover crops that build soil life make the ground less friendly to the fungus.
diseases.threshold: Walk banana blocks every 2 weeks and look for older leaves that yellow from the edge and hang down around the stem, or a split at the stem base. Cut a leaf stalk: brown or reddish streaks inside mean act on that plant the same day. One sick mat is already enough to act.

diseases.name: Banana bunchy top
diseases.hint: New leaves come out narrow, short and stiff, and they crowd together at the top of the plant.
diseases.no: No spray cures a bunchy top plant. Kill the aphids on it first, then destroy the whole mat and replant with virus tested plantlets.
avoid: Dimethoate
No spray cures the virus. To clear aphids from a sick mat before you destroy it, use a product named under banana aphid.
Acephate
No spray cures the virus. To clear aphids from a sick mat before you destroy it, use a product named under banana aphid.
prevent: Plant only virus tested tissue culture plantlets. Never take suckers from a bunched mat or from a farm where bunchy top is found.
On a sick mat, kill the aphids first with soap, oil or a banana aphid spray, then inject herbicide or dig out the whole mat and all its suckers.
Remove sick mats the same day you find them, then check the mats around them every week for the next months.
Prune extra suckers and keep weeds down around the mats. The aphids gather on young suckers.
Clear a hit area together with your neighbors, and replant only after every sick mat and stray sucker nearby is gone.
Abaca growers: rogue sick plants the same way and raise abaca nurseries far from infected banana and abaca fields.
bio: Ladybird beetles, hoverfly larvae, lacewings and small wasps eat the aphids, but they never stop the virus. Spray only the sick mat to spare them.
Soap or horticultural oil sprayed into the leaf throat and sheaths clears aphids from a sick mat before you remove it.
diseases.threshold: Check the youngest leaves of every mat each week or two for short dark green streaks like dots and dashes on the veins and leaf stalk, and for narrow, stiff, bunched new leaves. One such plant means act that day. Also look for dark aphid colonies at the stem base and inside the leaf sheaths of young suckers.

diseases.name: Black sigatoka
diseases.hint: Small reddish brown flecks appear first on the underside of young leaves.

banana: The backbone protectant: use it alone in drier weeks and mix it with every systemic spray. It can go in spray oil.
A strong protectant. Use it in water, not in spray oil, and keep it out of streams because it is toxic to fish.
Group 3: always mix with mancozeb or chlorothalonil, and keep group 3 to half the sprays of the year or fewer.
Group 11: at most 3 sprays a year, always mixed with a protectant, never two in a row.

Group 5 and good in spray oil, but it can harm an unborn child: wear full protection and keep pregnant women away.
Group 9: always mix with a protectant and keep it to half the sprays of the year or fewer.

Always mixed with a protectant and never two in a row.
Group 5: works well in spray oil. No more than 2 sprays in a row and half the program at most.
Group 7: at most 3 sprays a year, and a soil dose for nematodes counts as one of them.
Group 10: always mixed with a protectant, at most 3 sprays a year, never two in a row.
The difenoconazole does the work: count it as a group 3 spray, mix with a protectant and rotate.
Group 22: always mixed with a protectant, at most 4 sprays a year, never two in a row.

Group 21, a newer mode of action: at most 3 sprays a year, always mixed, never two in a row.

Counts as a group 11 and a group 7 spray: at most 3 a year, never two in a row.

Weaker on black sigatoka than mancozeb or chlorothalonil. Keep it as a minor partner only.
An old protectant that is harsh on skin and eyes. Mancozeb does the same job better.
A biological: fine inside a program in drier weeks, but alone it cannot hold black sigatoka in heavy rain.
An older group 3 fungicide. The newer ones in the same group work better.
A yeast extract that only wakes the plant's own defense. Use it inside a program, never alone.
Weak and short lived. At most a partner for organic farms in drier weeks, never the main spray in the rains.
Weak on black sigatoka. At most a minor partner in drier weeks.

A plant oil product: weak alone in the wet season. Keep it as a partner in a protectant program.
An older group 3 fungicide. The newer ones in the same group work better.

avoid: Iprodione
Its banana label is mainly for crown rot of the fruit. It does little against black sigatoka on the leaves.
Mineral oil
A spray oil: it carries the fungicide and slows the fungus a little, but alone it will not hold black sigatoka.
Isoprothiolane
A rice blast fungicide with no good proof against black sigatoka. Use a proven protectant instead.
Organosilicone surfactant plus non ionic surfactant
A wetting agent, not a fungicide: it only helps a real fungicide spread and stick.
Saponin (tea seed)
A tea seed extract that works mostly as a wetting agent. No good proof that it holds black sigatoka.
Non ionic surfactant plus c12 Fatty Acids
A wetting agent, not a fungicide: it only helps a real fungicide spread and stick.
prevent: Plant clean tissue culture plantlets on well drained land, with rows along the usual wind and wide spacing, so leaves dry fast after rain.
Every week in the wet months, cut off leaves more than half dead and cut out streaked parts. Take them out of the field or bury them.
Keep 3 or 4 plants per mat (the bearing plant, one follower and one or two small suckers) and remove the rest so air moves.
Keep weeds down, keep drains open and feed the plants well, with enough potash, so they hold their leaves longer.
After harvest, strip the dead leaves from the cut mother plant too. Old leaves on the ground feed the next wave of spores.
Where the disease is heavy, grow tolerant cooking banana types. Dessert types lose their leaves fastest.
bio: Bacillus based biologicals and tea tree oil products can fill drier weeks inside a program, but none holds black sigatoka alone in heavy rain.
diseases.threshold: Each week in the rainy months, count down from the newest open leaf (leaf 1) to the first leaf with dark streaks. The higher that number, the safer the plant. Act when streaks reach leaf 5 or a younger leaf, or when plants near flowering lose leaves fast, and cut away any leaf more than half dead.
diseases.rotate: This fungus resists group 1 (benomyl, thiophanate methyl) and group 11 (strobilurins) widely in Latin America and Africa. Philippine plantations still test sensitive, so keep it that way. Mix every systemic with mancozeb or chlorothalonil, never spray one group twice in a row, keep groups 1, 7, 11 and 21 to about 3 sprays a year each and group 3 to 8, never over half of all sprays.

diseases.name: Moko disease and bugtok of banana
diseases.local: Bugtok is also called tapurok, in saba and cardaba.
diseases.hint: On Cavendish and other dessert bananas, leaves turn yellow and then wilt.
diseases.no: No spray cures it. Kill and remove sick mats, disinfect tools between plants, and bag the bunch and remove the male bud early.
prevent: Plant tissue culture plantlets or suckers from a farm known to be clean. Never take suckers or fruit from a farm with moko or bugtok.
Kill a sick mat where it stands with herbicide, together with the healthy looking mats right beside it, and leave the dead plants to dry in place.
Dip cutting tools in household bleach mixed with water between mats when you desucker, deleaf or harvest, and keep a separate knife for sick areas.
For bugtok in saba and cardaba, bag the young bunch and snap off the male bud with a forked stick once the last hand opens, so insects cannot carry the bacterium in.
Keep sick block water, soil and trash out of drains and canals, and pull weeds and heliconia that can hide the bacterium.
After a sick crop, leave the spot fallow or under a legume cover crop for at least 12 months before banana goes back.
diseases.threshold: Walk the farm every week and cut open any plant that yellows and wilts or any bunch with fingers that ripen unevenly: brown stained flesh, a brown core or sticky ooze at the cut means a sick mat. One sick mat is enough to act the same day.

diseases.name: Papaya ringspot
diseases.hint: The leaves get a mottled mosaic of bright yellow and green.
diseases.no: No spray cures it, and insecticides rarely help: aphids pass the virus in a few seconds of probing, before any spray can kill them.
prevent: Raise seedlings under fine net or buy from a nursery you trust, and check each seedling for mosaic before planting.
Plant new papaya far from old papaya and from squash, melon and other cucurbits, and time planting for months when aphids are fewer.
Pull sick trees and stray papaya seedlings at once, and end badly hit blocks. They feed the virus and aphids to the rest.
Plant two or more rows of corn or another tall crop around the papaya block so passing aphids probe there first and lose the virus.
Wash knives between trees, keep weeds down, and grow tolerant or resistant varieties where you can get them.
bio: Ladybird beetles, hoverflies and small wasps keep aphid numbers down, but no natural enemy is fast enough to stop the virus.
diseases.threshold: Inspect every tree each week in the first months: look for yellow mosaic on the young leaves, oily streaks on leaf stalks and stems, and rings on the fruit. Pull a tree at the first signs while sick trees are still few. Once most of a block shows rings, end that block and replant away from it.

diseases.name: Coconut cadang cadang
diseases.local: In Bicol the disease is called gadan gadan, which means dead or dying.
diseases.hint: Yellow, or chlorotic, spots appear on the leaves.
diseases.no: No spray or injection cures it. Remove sick palms, clean tools between palms and never move planting material out of a hit area.
prevent: Have a suspect palm tested first, then cut down and burn the palms confirmed sick so they stop being a source.
Clean bolos, knives, scythes and climbing gear between palms, for example with household bleach mixed with water.
Never move seedlings, nuts or palm parts from an area with cadang cadang to a clean area, and respect the quarantine checkpoints.
Replant cleared spots with healthy seedlings from a clean area so the farm keeps producing.
Keep the farm in good care, but know that only the removal of sick palms takes the source away.
diseases.threshold: Look over each palm every few months for small yellow spots on the fronds, round and scarred nuts, and fewer and smaller nuts. A palm with these signs should be tested before you act, since many causes look alike.

diseases.name: Coconut bud rot
diseases.hint: The spear leaf wilts or bends over, and may turn light green.

coconut: Given by trunk injection, it protects the bud of palms at risk. It cannot save a palm whose spear has already rotted.

prevent: Open drains in low, wet parts of the farm and avoid planting coconut where water stands after rain.
Do not crowd the palms, and clear trash around young palms, so air moves through the crowns and they dry after rain.
Cut down and burn a palm with a rotten bud as soon as you find it, so its spores do not reach the neighbors.
Keep nurseries clean and drained, do not crowd the seedlings, and pull out and burn any sick seedling.
Keep rhinoceros beetle and palm weevil damage down. Their holes in the crown let water and the water mold in.
Plant hybrids or tall types in wet areas. Pure dwarf types catch bud rot most easily.
diseases.threshold: After heavy rain or a typhoon, check young palms for a spear leaf that wilts, yellows, bends over or pulls out easily with a foul smell. Act on the first such palm at once and protect the palms around it.

diseases.name: Citrus greening
diseases.hint: Leaves show a blotchy mottle, with yellow and green patches in an uneven pattern.
diseases.no: No spray cures a greening tree. Plant clean seedlings, keep psyllids off the new flushes and remove sick trees.
prevent: Plant only certified disease free seedlings raised in insect proof screen houses. Never graft budwood from a tree that shows signs.
Every month in greening areas, look for blotchy mottled leaves, yellow shoots and small lopsided fruit. Kill the psyllids on a sick tree, then remove and burn it.
Keep kamuning (orange jasmine) and curry leaf away from citrus. Both host the psyllid and the greening bacterium.
Never bring citrus plants or budwood from greening areas into clean ones, and keep a record of where each tree came from.
Replant a block all at once with clean trees, and work with neighbors so psyllids from abandoned trees do not reinfect them.
Feed and water trees well. It does not cure greening, but it keeps lightly hit trees bearing longer.
bio: Ladybird beetles, hoverfly larvae, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps kill psyllid nymphs. Spare them by spraying only flushes that carry psyllids.
Horticultural oil, neem or soap sprays on new flushes cut psyllid numbers with less harm to these enemies.
diseases.threshold: Check the new flushes every week or two while trees push new growth: look for small brown psyllids resting with the tail raised at a slant, and for white waxy threads from the nymphs. In an area with greening, any psyllid on young trees or nursery stock is reason to act, and any tree with blotchy mottle should be checked and removed.
diseases.rotate: Psyllids abroad have lost sensitivity to imidacloprid after years of heavy use. Do not lean on group 4A alone, and swap to another group named under the psyllid between flushes.

diseases.name: Black pod of cacao
diseases.hint: Small brown, oily spots appear on the pod and spread quickly.

cacao: Protects only the pod skin it covers: keep the young and ripening pods covered through the rains and spray again after heavy rain.
Moves inside the tree and works best as a trunk treatment before the main rains. Pod removal is still needed.
Protects only the pod skin it covers: keep the young and ripening pods covered through the rains and spray again after heavy rain.

prevent: Prune to an open canopy, remove water shoots and low branches, and thin the shade so sun and wind dry the pods after rain.
Space cacao at least 3 meters apart and avoid heavy clay and wet spots where water stands after rain.
Harvest ripe pods on time and pick every black pod each round. Bury or burn sick pods and empty husks away from the trees.
Mulch the bare ground under the trees. Rain splash from bare soil throws the water mold up onto the low pods.
Keep rats and squirrels down, since they chew sick pods and carry the water mold to healthy ones, and clean knives between trees.
Plant tolerant clones when you replant or rehabilitate old trees.
bio: Trichoderma sprays on pods have been tried abroad. They help a little but never replace picking the sick pods.
diseases.threshold: In the wet season, check the pods every week. Act at the first brown spots: pick every sick pod on each round, every week or two in the main crop, and keep the healthy pods covered before rain.

diseases.name: Coffee leaf rust
diseases.hint: Small spots of about 2 to 3 mm appear and grow to about 15 mm.

coffee: A protectant: spray before the rains and cover the leaf undersides. Copper can also kill the fungus that keeps green scale in check.
A protectant: spray before the rains and cover the leaf undersides. Copper can also kill the fungus that keeps green scale in check.
A home made copper that must be mixed fresh and right, or it scorches the leaves. Ready copper products are easier.

prevent: When you replant, choose rust resistant or tolerant coffee and clean seedlings. Arabica at low and middle elevations suffers most.
Give light, even shade and prune every year so leaves dry quickly after rain. Heavy shade keeps leaves wet and feeds the rust.
Feed the trees well, above all in heavy bearing years. Trees that bear heavily on poor soil drop their leaves to rust first.
Space trees so air moves through the rows and keep the farm weeded.
Renew old, exhausted trees by stumping. Young vigorous growth stands rust better.
bio: A white fungus (Lecanicillium) often grows over old rust spots and slows the rust. It is a friend, not a new disease.
diseases.threshold: From the start of the rains, check the undersides of lower and middle leaves on trees across the farm every two weeks for yellow orange powdery spots. Start protecting as soon as spots appear in a heavily bearing block. Once many leaves have fallen, sprays come too late for that season.

diseases.name: Southern corn leaf blight
diseases.hint: Small tan to brown oblong spots between the leaf veins that join into large dead patches across the leaf.

sources.label: DA Caraga Corn Program, Mga Kasagarang Sakit sa Mais (Technoguide 27, 2021)

corn_yellow: Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
corn_sweet: Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
corn_glutinous: Both parts are group 3: alternate it with a strobilurin mix rather than spraying it again and again.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.
Group 11 alone carries a resistance risk: spray it at most twice a season, alternating with group 3.
A protectant: it only guards leaves it covers before infection, and rain washes it off.

prevent: Plant a resistant hybrid. It is the main control in hot, wet lowlands.
Plow under or remove corn residue after harvest, where the fungus survives.
Rotate with a crop that is not a grass, and clear volunteer corn.
Feed balanced nitrogen with enough potassium. Weak, hungry plants blight faster.
Avoid planting so late that the crop flowers in the hottest, wettest weeks.
diseases.threshold: In hot, wet weather, check the lower and middle leaves on 20 plants at each of five spots every week from the 8 leaf stage. Spray a susceptible hybrid when spots climb from the lower leaves toward the ear leaf before silking. After the dough stage a spray does not pay.

diseases.name: Grain mold of sorghum
diseases.sci: Fusarium spp., Curvularia lunata, Alternaria spp. and other fungi
diseases.hint: Grains turn pink, white and fluffy, or black when rain falls during flowering and grain filling, and they crumble at threshing.

sources.label: TNAU Agritech, Grain mould of sorghum

prevent: Time planting so the grain fills and ripens in dry weather.
Choose varieties with hard, colored grain or loose heads, which mold less.
Harvest at maturity without delay, and dry the grain down to 12 to 13 percent moisture.
Control head bugs and caterpillars that break the grain open for the fungi.
Rotate with a crop that is not a grass, and clean up crop residue.
diseases.threshold: In wet weather from flowering to grain fill, check 20 heads at each of five spots twice a week. A protectant spray at flowering helps only a little. When mold shows, harvest as soon as the grain is mature, marked by a black spot at the grain base, and dry it fast.

diseases.name: Southern blight (stem rot)
diseases.hint: A branch or the whole plant wilts, and white cottony threads with small round seed like balls cover the stem at the soil line.

sources.label: Pacific Pests and Pathogens, Peanut southern blight
PhilFIDA, Technoguide on Cotton Pests and their Management
EWS Plant Doctor, Southern blight
DA RFO 02, Tomato Production Guide

avoid: Carbendazim
Southern blight shrugs off carbendazim and its kin. This group does not control it.
prevent: Plow deep before planting to bury the seed like balls, which die when buried well below the surface.
Rotate with corn, rice or other grasses. A flooded rice crop kills many of the resting balls.
Keep mulch, dead leaves and soil heaped up off the stem base, and do not wound stems when weeding.
Pull sick plants with the soil around them and destroy them away from the field.
Solarize seedbeds and small plots under clear plastic for 4 to 6 weeks in the dry season.
bio: Trichoderma mixed into compost and placed in the planting hole or at the stem base helps hold southern blight down.
diseases.threshold: In hot, wet weeks look at the stem base of every wilting plant for white cottony threads and small round brown balls like mustard seed. Pull the first sick plants with the soil around them. A soil drench at the stem base pays only on high value crops with many sick plants.

diseases.name: Stem rot and charcoal rot
diseases.hint: Dark brown sunken patches circle the stem near the soil, peppered with tiny black dots, and the plant wilts and breaks.

sources.label: FAO AGRIS: IPM module against stem rot and insect pests of jute (Corchorus olitorius)

prevent: Do not let the crop run dry at flowering and pod filling. Charcoal rot strikes plants under heat and drought stress.
Plant clean seed, treated with Trichoderma where you can.
Rotate with rice or other grains. A flooded rice crop clears much of the fungus from the soil.
Do not sow too thick, and keep potash up so plants stand the heat better.
Remove and burn sick plants and stubble after harvest, and work compost into the soil.
bio: Coat the seed with Trichoderma before sowing, or mix it into compost for the planting rows.
diseases.threshold: In hot, dry spells split the lower stem of plants that wilt and dry early. A grey inside peppered with tiny black dots confirms it. There is no spray threshold: plan clean or treated seed and watering for the next crop.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.hint: Raised reddish brown pustules ringed with yellow form on the leaf underside and rub off as a rusty powder.

sources.label: DA RFO 02 Cagayan Valley, Snap Beans Production Guide

stringbean: A protectant: start at the first pustules, before rust covers the leaves, and spray again after heavy rain.
Copper is weak on rust. Mancozeb or chlorothalonil protect better.
Copper is weak on rust. Mancozeb or chlorothalonil protect better.
Weak on rust. Mancozeb or chlorothalonil protect better.
Weak on rust. It only slows the first pustules and must be repeated often.

A biological with weak action on rust. It fits only very light attacks in organic plots.
cowpea: A protectant: start at the first pustules, before rust covers the leaves, and spray again after heavy rain.
Copper is weak on rust. Mancozeb or chlorothalonil protect better.

mungbean: A protectant: start at the first pustules, before rust covers the leaves, and spray again after heavy rain.
Copper is weak on rust. Mancozeb or chlorothalonil protect better.

Weak on rust. Mancozeb or chlorothalonil protect better.

Copper is weak on rust. Mancozeb or chlorothalonil protect better.

prevent: Plant a rust resistant or tolerant variety where one suits your area.
Do not plant a new crop beside an old rusty one, and pull volunteer bean plants. Spores blow from old plantings to new.
Space the rows so leaves dry fast, and do not water over the leaves late in the day.
Plow under or remove old vines and leaves right after the last picking.
Rotate with crops outside the bean family for at least a season.
diseases.threshold: From the first flowers, check the underside of the older leaves every week. Start spraying when the first rusty pustules show and the weather stays humid. A crop already near its last picking rarely pays for a spray.

diseases.name: Bean and cowpea mosaic
diseases.sci: Bean common mosaic virus, Cowpea aphid borne mosaic virus
diseases.hint: Leaves show light and dark green patches, pucker and curl down, and the pods are few and twisted.
diseases.no: No spray cures it, and aphids pass the virus in seconds, before any insecticide acts. Plant clean seed, pull sick plants early and keep new plantings away from old ones.

sources.label: Pacific Pests and Pathogens, Bean common mosaic

prevent: Plant clean seed, and never save seed from plants with mottled, curled or blistered leaves. Both viruses travel in seed.
Grow a resistant variety where one is sold.
Pull mottled plants as soon as you see them, before aphids carry the virus to their neighbors.
Keep new plantings away from older bean and cowpea fields, and clear legume weeds and volunteers.
Plant a border of corn or sorghum around the field and use silver mulch to keep winged aphids off.
bio: Ladybirds, hoverfly larvae and small parasitic wasps hold aphids down. Avoid broad sprays that kill them.
diseases.threshold: Check growing tips and young pods twice a week for aphid colonies, most of all in the first month. Spraying the aphids does little against this virus, so put the effort into clean seed and early roguing.

diseases.name: Early and late leaf spot of peanut
diseases.hint: Brown spots with a yellow ring, or dark brown to black spots on the leaf underside, and the leaves drop early.

sources.label: Peanut CRSP Philippines, Peanut production guide (M. K. Palomar, editor)

peanut: Peanut leaf spot fungi resist this group in many places after heavy use: no more than two sprays, in turn with a protectant.
Copper is weaker on peanut leaf spot than chlorothalonil or mancozeb.

prevent: Rotate for two to three years with corn, rice or other grains, and bury or remove peanut residue after harvest.
Pull volunteer peanut plants, which carry the fungus from one season to the next.
Plant a tolerant variety where one suits your area, and plant early in the season when you can.
Space the rows so the canopy dries fast, and feed the crop with balanced fertilizer and enough calcium.
diseases.threshold: From about 30 days after sowing, check the lower leaves every week. Start sprays when the first spots show on the lower leaves in wet weather, and keep the leaves covered while the pods fill.
diseases.rotate: Peanut leaf spot fungi became resistant to benomyl and its kin (FRAC 1) within a few seasons of heavy use in several countries. Turn thiophanate methyl with chlorothalonil or mancozeb and never spray it alone season after season.

diseases.name: Peanut rust
diseases.hint: Tiny orange to reddish brown pustules under the older leaves break open and shed a rusty powder.

sources.label: Peanut CRSP Philippines, Peanut production guide (M. K. Palomar, editor)

peanut: A protectant: start at the first orange pustules, and keep the leaves covered while the pods fill.

prevent: Plant a rust tolerant variety where one suits your area.
Pull volunteer peanut plants between seasons. They carry rust from one crop to the next.
Plant at the same time as your neighbors so no field stays green for rust to jump to.
Rotate with grains and bury the old crop residue after harvest.
diseases.threshold: From flowering, check the underside of the lower leaves every week. Start spraying at the first orange pustules if the crop still has more than a month to go before harvest.

diseases.name: Soybean rust
diseases.hint: Tiny tan to reddish brown spots with raised pustules on the underside of the lower leaves, which yellow and drop early.

sources.label: Asian soybean rust review, notes yield losses up to 80 percent in the Philippines (PMC)

soybean: A protectant: spray at the first pustules and keep the leaves covered. It cannot clear rust already spread.
A protectant: spray at the first pustules and keep the leaves covered. It cannot clear rust already spread.
Copper is weak on soybean rust. Chlorothalonil or mancozeb protect better.
Copper is weak on soybean rust. Chlorothalonil or mancozeb protect better.
Weak on soybean rust. Chlorothalonil or mancozeb protect better.
Weak on soybean rust. It only slows the first pustules and must be repeated often.
Copper is weak on soybean rust. Chlorothalonil or mancozeb protect better.

prevent: Plant early in the season and avoid late plantings that fill pods in the wettest months.
Grow a tolerant or early maturing variety where one suits your area.
Pull volunteer soybean and clear wild legume vines such as kudzu near the field. They keep the rust alive between crops.
Plant at the same time as your neighbors, and do not plant beside an older rusty field.
Space the rows so the canopy dries quickly after rain.
diseases.threshold: From flowering, check the underside of the lower and middle leaves every week with a hand lens for tiny tan pustules. Start sprays at the first pustules, since rust spreads fast in humid weather and the loss comes from early leaf drop.
diseases.rotate: Soybean rust has grown resistant to triazoles (FRAC 3), strobilurins (FRAC 11) and SDHIs (FRAC 7) in South America and elsewhere. Use those groups only in mixes with mancozeb or chlorothalonil, and never the same group twice in a row.

diseases.name: False rust of winged bean (orange gall)
diseases.hint: Small bright orange yellow raised galls cover the leaves, stems and pods, which twist and curl when badly hit.
diseases.no: No spray is proven against it. Plant tolerant varieties, pick off galled parts, space the vines for air and save seed only from clean plants.

sources.label: PROSEA, Psophocarpus tetragonolobus (winged bean)
PestNet, false rust (Synchytrium psophocarpi) on winged bean

prevent: Plant a tolerant variety, and save seed only from clean, healthy plants.
Trellis and space the vines so air moves and the leaves dry quickly.
Avoid shady, damp corners of the farm for winged bean.
Pick off galled shoots and pods early, and burn the old vines after the last harvest.
Do not plant a new crop beside an old infected one, and rotate the patch with other crops.
diseases.threshold: In cool, wet weather check young shoots, leaves and pods twice a week for raised orange galls. Pick and burn galled parts as soon as they show.

diseases.name: Pigeon pea wilt
diseases.hint: Plants yellow and wilt one by one, often at flowering and podding, with a purple band at the stem base and brown streaks inside the stem.
diseases.no: No spray saves a wilting plant. Plant resistant varieties, treat seed with Trichoderma and rotate with grains.

sources.label: Journal of Biological Control, Management of pigeonpea wilt caused by Fusarium udum through integrated approaches

prevent: Plant a wilt resistant variety. It is the main answer to this disease.
Rotate for three years with sorghum, corn or other grains, or intercrop pigeon pea with sorghum.
Use clean seed from healthy fields, treated with Trichoderma before sowing.
Pull and burn wilted plants with their roots, and do not leave infected stubble in the field.
Drain the field well. Waterlogged soil makes the wilt worse.
bio: Coat the seed with Trichoderma viride or Trichoderma harzianum before sowing, and add it to compost for the rows.
diseases.threshold: Walk the field from flowering and look for plants that wilt and dry in patches, with a purple band up the stem and brown streaks inside. Pull and burn them. There is no spray threshold.

diseases.name: Storage rot of root crops
diseases.sci: Lasiodiplodia theobromae, Fusarium spp., Penicillium spp., Rhizopus stolonifer
diseases.hint: Stored tubers and roots soften, turn brown or black inside and grow white, green or black mold, starting at cuts and bruises.
diseases.no: Sprays do not save stored roots. Dig with care, cure them in the shade, keep only sound ones and store them dry and airy.

sources.label: PROSEA: Dioscorea alata (purple yam)
DA RFO 2 Sweet Potato Production Guide

prevent: Dig with care so the skin is not cut or bruised, and harvest in dry weather.
Cure sweet potato, ubi and taro in the shade for a few days before storing, so small wounds heal over.
Sell or process cassava within two or three days of digging. It spoils fast once out of the ground.
Store only sound roots in a clean, dry, airy and shaded place, off the floor.
Keep sweet potato weevil out of the field and the store, since its holes let the rot fungi in.
diseases.threshold: Sort stored roots and tubers every week, and take out any soft, moldy, sunken or sour smelling one at once before it spreads.

diseases.name: Rhizome and corm rot
diseases.sci: Pythium aphanidermatum, Pythium myriotylum and other Pythium spp. (often with Fusarium spp.)
diseases.hint: Lower leaves yellow, shoots fall over at the collar, and the rhizome or corm turns soft, watery, brown and foul smelling.

sources.label: DA CAR Technoguide: production and management of ginger
Vikaspedia: pests and diseases management in ginger

prevent: Plant seed rhizomes and corms only from healthy fields, and throw out any piece that is soft, brown or shrunken.
Plant on raised beds with deep drains. Standing water is what this rot needs.
Rotate for at least three years away from ginger, turmeric and taro, and do not plant where the rot struck before.
Mulch with green leaves after planting, and work in plenty of well rotted compost.
Keep rhizome fly, scale and root knot nematodes down, since their wounds let the rot in.
Lift and destroy rotted clumps with the soil around them, and never carry soil from a sick bed to a clean one.
bio: Mix Trichoderma into compost and add it at planting and again at the first hilling up. It guards the rhizomes against Pythium.
diseases.threshold: From two months after planting, watch for lower leaves yellowing from the tips and a soft, water soaked collar. Pull one clump to check the rhizome. Remove sick clumps with the soil around them at once and treat the spot and the plants around it.
diseases.rotate: Pythium can become resistant to metalaxyl (FRAC 4) when it is used every season. Use it only as a seed dip or a first drench and lean on drainage and Trichoderma.

diseases.name: Sweet potato scab
diseases.hint: Small corky brown scabs form on leaf veins and vines, and young leaves curl, twist and stay small.

sources.label: DA RFO 2 Sweet Potato Production Guide
Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Sweetpotato scab

avoid: Maneb
No maneb product is on the Philippine list. Use mancozeb instead.
prevent: Plant a scab resistant variety. It is the main answer in wet, upland areas.
Take cuttings only from healthy, scab free fields, and use the young tip cuttings.
Rotate with other crops and do not plant beside an older field with scab.
Remove and bury old vines after harvest.
diseases.threshold: In wet weather check young leaves and vine tips every week for small, raised, corky spots and puckered, curled leaves. Pull the first sick hills. A spray pays only in a nursery where you cut planting vines.

diseases.name: Sweet potato virus disease
diseases.sci: Virus complex: sweet potato feathery mottle virus, sweet potato chlorotic stunt virus and others
diseases.hint: Leaves show vein clearing, mosaic or purple veins, turn small, crinkled and misshapen, and vines are stunted with short joints.
diseases.no: No spray cures a virus. Plant clean cuttings, pull out sick plants and volunteers, and keep aphids and whiteflies down.

sources.label: DA RFO 2 Sweet Potato Production Guide

prevent: Plant cuttings from clean, virus tested nurseries, or from the healthiest plants of your own field.
Pull sick plants and volunteers early, before the insects carry the virus on.
Keep new plantings away from old sweet potato fields, and clear morning glory type weeds nearby.
Renew your planting stock every few seasons instead of cutting from the same old field again and again.
Grow a tolerant variety where one suits your area.
bio: Ladybirds, lacewings and small parasitic wasps hold aphids and whiteflies down. Avoid broad sprays that kill them.
diseases.threshold: In the first two months check the planting every two weeks and pull any stunted plant with mottled, yellow veined or crinkled leaves. Spraying the aphids does little, since they pass the virus within seconds. Put the effort into clean cuttings.

diseases.name: Sweet potato little leaf
diseases.hint: Vines turn bushy with many side shoots and tiny pale leaves, and the plant forms few or no roots.
diseases.no: No spray cures it. Plant cuttings only from healthy fields, pull and burn bushy plants, and do not plant beside a sick field.

sources.label: Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Sweetpotato little leaf
EPPO Global Database: sweet potato little leaf phytoplasma, Philippines

prevent: Take cuttings only from healthy fields with no bushy, little leaf plants.
Pull and burn sick hills as soon as you see them, before leafhoppers carry it on.
Do not plant beside a sick field, and clear volunteers and morning glory weeds around it.
Rotate the field with grains for a season after an outbreak.
diseases.threshold: Walk the field every two weeks and pull and burn any hill with tiny, pale, crowded leaves on short vines.

diseases.name: Cassava witches broom
diseases.sci: Phytoplasma (Candidatus Phytoplasma luffae group); the fungus Ceratobasidium theobromae is also found in sick plants
diseases.hint: Many thin shoots bunch at the top like a broom, leaves turn small and yellow, stems dry back, and roots stay small with brown streaks inside.
diseases.no: No spray cures it. It travels mainly in infected stakes, so plant cuttings only from healthy fields and pull and burn broomed plants.

sources.label: Status of Cassava Witches Broom Disease in the Philippines (Plants, 2024)

prevent: Plant stakes only from healthy fields that showed no broomed plants.
Pull and burn broomed plants with their stems, and never cut planting stakes from them.
Do not bring stakes from areas where the disease is known.
Clean cutting tools between plants when you gather stakes.
diseases.threshold: Walk the field every month and pull and burn any plant with crowded, thin shoots and small leaves at the top. Check stakes before planting and throw out any with dark streaks inside.

diseases.name: Taro leaf blight
diseases.hint: Round purple brown spots with a yellow edge ooze yellow drops and spread fast in rainy weather until the whole leaf collapses.

sources.label: Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Taro leaf blight

prevent: Plant a tolerant variety where one suits your area, and use clean planting tops and suckers from healthy fields.
Space the plants wider so the leaves dry fast, and avoid overhead watering.
Pick off and destroy spotted leaves early and often during wet spells.
Plant so the crop matures in the drier months where you can, and do not plant beside an older infected field.
Remove old leaves and plant debris after harvest, and rotate the field when you can.
diseases.threshold: In warm, wet weeks check the leaves twice a week for round, purple brown, water soaked spots that weep orange drops. Pick off the first spotted leaves at once, and start protectant sprays when spots show on many plants in the rainy season.
diseases.rotate: Taro leaf blight has shown resistance to metalaxyl (FRAC 4) where it was used alone. Mix or alternate it with mancozeb, copper or phosphorous acid (FRAC P07).

diseases.name: Potato cyst nematode
diseases.hint: Plants grow in stunted yellow patches that wilt at midday, and pinhead sized white to golden cysts cling to the roots.

sources.label: Benguet State University policy brief: potato cyst nematode and bacterial wilt in Benguet
BPI Baguio addresses bacterial wilt and potato cyst nematode

potato: An organophosphate: put it in the soil at planting only, wear full protection, and keep it away from streams.

prevent: Plant only certified seed potatoes, and never bring seed or soil from fields known to carry the nematode.
Wash soil off tillers, tools, boots and sacks before moving between farms. The cysts travel in soil.
Rotate for at least five years away from potato and tomato, with cabbage, carrot, beans or grains.
Plant a potato variety resistant to the golden cyst nematode where one is sold.
Pull volunteer potatoes and nightshade weeds, which keep the nematode multiplying.
bio: Products with the fungus Purpureocillium lilacinus can lower egg numbers a little. They do not replace a long rotation.
diseases.threshold: Look for patches of stunted, yellowing plants, then dig one at flowering and look for tiny white to golden pinhead cysts on the roots. Once a field has cysts, do not plant potato there again without a soil test showing low egg numbers.

diseases.name: Carrot leaf blight
diseases.hint: Dark brown spots with yellow edges start on older leaves and stalks, then join until the tops blacken and dry as if scorched.

sources.label: Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Carrot leaf spot

carrot: Copper is weaker on Alternaria leaf blight than chlorothalonil. It fits best when bacterial leaf blight is also present.
Copper is weaker on Alternaria leaf blight than chlorothalonil. It fits best when bacterial leaf blight is also present.
Copper is weaker on Alternaria leaf blight than chlorothalonil. It fits best when bacterial leaf blight is also present.

prevent: Sow clean seed. Soak doubtful seed in hot water at 50 degrees Celsius for 20 minutes before sowing.
Rotate for two to three years away from carrot and celery, and plow under or remove the tops after harvest.
Thin the rows so air moves, and water in the morning by furrow or at the base.
Feed the crop evenly through the season. Stressed, hungry plants blight first.
Grow a tolerant variety where one suits your area.
diseases.threshold: Check the older leaves every week from about six weeks after sowing. Start protectant sprays when dark spots with yellow edges show on a few plants in warm, wet weather, so the tops stay strong enough to pull at harvest.

diseases.name: Ginger leaf spot
diseases.hint: Small water soaked spots on the leaves grow into yellowish then brown spots with white centers that run together.

sources.label: Vikaspedia: pests and diseases management in ginger

ginger: The label names Cercospora leaf spot. It works on ginger leaf spots too, but change group after one or two sprays.

prevent: Plant healthy seed rhizomes from fields free of leaf spot.
Space the rows and mulch the beds so rain does not splash spores onto the lower leaves.
Pick off and burn spotted leaves early, and clear old leaves after harvest.
Rotate away from ginger and turmeric for two to three years.
Feed the crop with balanced fertilizer and enough potash.
diseases.threshold: In the rainy months check the leaves every week. Start spraying when small oval spots with pale centers and yellow halos show on many plants, before they join into dry patches.

diseases.name: Mosaic viruses of squash and gourds
diseases.sci: Zucchini yellow mosaic virus, Papaya ringspot virus type W, Cucumber mosaic virus, Watermelon mosaic virus; on sayote, Chayote mosaic virus
diseases.hint: Leaves turn mottled yellow and green with blisters, stay small and twisted, and fruits come out bumpy or spotted.
diseases.no: No spray cures a virus. Pull sick vines early, keep aphids off young plants, clear weedy hosts and plant tolerant varieties.

sources.label: DA RFO 02, Squash Production Guide
EWS Plant Doctor, Zucchini yellow mosaic
NORDIS, BSU on chayote mosaic virus in Benguet

prevent: Plant a tolerant variety where one is sold.
Pull and burn mottled, stunted vines as soon as you see them.
Keep new plantings away from older squash, melon and gourd fields, and clear weedy cucurbit hosts around the farm.
Use silver reflective mulch and a border of corn around the field to keep winged aphids off the young vines.
Raise seedlings under net, and plant a new crop only after the old one is plowed under.
bio: Ladybirds, hoverfly larvae and small parasitic wasps hold aphids down. Avoid broad sprays that kill them.
diseases.threshold: Check the underside of young leaves twice a week in the first month for winged aphids and new colonies. Spraying aphids does little against these viruses, so put the effort into clean seedlings, mulch and barriers.

diseases.name: Alternaria leaf spot of the cabbage family
diseases.hint: Round brown to black spots with rings like a target and a yellow halo appear on older leaves, and heads may show dark specks.

sources.label: Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Cabbage black leaf spot

cabbage: It moves into the leaf and stops new spots. Turn it with mancozeb so the fungus does not adapt.
A biological: start before the spots spread. It holds light attacks, not a heavy one.
Copper is weak on Alternaria. It fits only where black rot or downy mildew is the bigger worry.
Copper is weak on Alternaria. It fits only where black rot or downy mildew is the bigger worry.
Copper is weak on Alternaria. It fits only where black rot or downy mildew is the bigger worry.
An old triazole that is weaker on Alternaria than difenoconazole or tebuconazole.
cauliflower: Copper is weak on Alternaria. It fits only where black rot or downy mildew is the bigger worry.

avoid: Benomyl
Alternaria fungi are hardly touched by benomyl and its kin. Use mancozeb or a triazole for this leaf spot.
Thiophanate methyl
Alternaria fungi are hardly touched by this group. Use mancozeb or a triazole for this leaf spot.
prevent: Sow clean seed. Soak doubtful seed in hot water at 50 degrees Celsius for 25 minutes before sowing.
Rotate for three years away from the cabbage family, and pull mustard family weeds near the field.
Plow under or remove crop residue right after harvest.
Space plants so the leaves dry quickly, and water at the base in the morning.
Feed the crop evenly with enough potash. Stressed and old leaves spot first.
bio: Bacillus based biofungicides help as protectants when sprayed before spots spread.
diseases.threshold: Check the outer leaves every week from transplanting. Start protectant sprays when brown target spots show on the lower leaves in wet weather, and keep spots off the heads and the seed pods in the weeks before harvest.

diseases.name: Thrips borne mottle and spotted wilt viruses
diseases.sci: Watermelon silver mottle virus, Melon yellow spot virus, Tomato spotted wilt virus (tospoviruses)
diseases.hint: Leaves show pale flecks, rings or silvery mottling, shoot tips stand up stiff, and plants infected young stay small and bear little.
diseases.no: No spray cures the virus. Control thrips early, pull sick plants, and clear weeds and old crop debris after harvest.

sources.label: EWS Plant Doctor, Tospovirus
EWS Plant Doctor, Watermelon diseases and pests

prevent: Raise seedlings under fine insect net, and plant only seedlings without thrips or spotted, bronzed leaves.
Pull and destroy plants with ring spots, bronzing or yellow mottling as soon as you see them.
Clear weeds around the field and plow under old crops right after harvest. Both keep thrips and the virus alive.
Do not plant a new melon or pepper crop beside an older infected one, and leave a gap between crops when you can.
Use silver reflective mulch and blue sticky traps to keep thrips numbers down.
Plant a tolerant variety where one is sold.
bio: Predatory mites and minute pirate bugs eat thrips. Avoid broad sprays that kill them.
Beauveria or Metarhizium sprays on flowers and young leaves lower thrips numbers, not the virus in sick plants.
diseases.threshold: Twice a week tap flowers and young leaves over a white tray and count the thrips, from the seedbed to the first month after transplanting. Act early on thrips in young plants, since plants infected young lose the most.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.sci: Albugo candida (cabbage family), Albugo ipomoeae aquaticae (kangkong)
diseases.hint: Raised white blisters under the leaves burst into white powder, with yellow patches above and twisted, swollen shoots.

sources.label: Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Cabbage white rust (also kangkong)

prevent: Sow clean seed, and plant kangkong cuttings only from healthy beds.
Rotate for two years away from the cabbage family, and away from kangkong for kangkong beds.
Remove infected leaves and plants early, and clear crop residue after harvest.
Pull wild mustards and wild morning glory weeds that carry the same fungus.
Space the plants and water at the base in the morning so leaves dry before night.
diseases.threshold: In cool, humid weeks check the underside of leaves twice a week for white, blister like pustules. Pick off the first infected leaves, and start protectant sprays when pustules show on many plants.

diseases.name: Phytophthora blight
diseases.hint: Black lesions climb the stem from the base, the crown rots and the whole plant wilts, and fruits rot under white mold in wet weather.

sources.label: EWS Plant Doctor, Phytophthora blight
EWS Plant Doctor, Eggplant diseases and pests

chili: Works as a soil drench at the stem base and on the leaves. Turn it with another water mold group so the mold does not adapt.
Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.
bellpepper: Works as a soil drench at the stem base and on the leaves. Turn it with another water mold group so the mold does not adapt.
Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.
eggplant: Works as a soil drench at the stem base and on the leaves. Turn it with another water mold group so the mold does not adapt.
Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.
Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.
squash: Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.
Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.
watermelon: Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.
Protects leaves and fruit only. It does nothing for the root and crown rot that kills the plant.

prevent: Plant on high, rounded beds with open drains. The mold swims in standing water.
Water by drip or furrow, never flood the beds, and mulch to stop soil splashing onto fruit.
Rotate for three years away from pepper, eggplant, tomato and cucurbits.
Graft pepper onto a resistant rootstock where one is sold, or plant a tolerant variety.
Pull sick plants with the soil around them, and never let water run from a sick field into a clean one.
bio: Trichoderma mixed into compost at planting helps protect the roots and stem base.
diseases.threshold: After heavy rain or flooding, walk the low spots daily for wilting plants with a dark, water soaked stem base and fruit with greasy grey mold. Pull sick plants at once with the soil around them, and drench the plants around them while the soil stays wet.
diseases.rotate: Phytophthora capsici often resists metalaxyl (FRAC 4) in Asia and elsewhere, so do not count on it. Turn the water mold groups (28, 40, 43, 21, 49) and keep drainage the main tool.

diseases.name: Choanephora wet rot
diseases.hint: Flowers and young fruits turn soft and wet, then grow whiskers of fungus with tiny black heads, like a pincushion.

sources.label: EWS Plant Doctor, Choanephora wet rot
EWS Plant Doctor, Eggplant diseases and pests
DA RFO 02, Upo Production Guide

prevent: Space plants and trellis vines so flowers and young fruit dry quickly after rain.
Pick off old, fading flowers and rotting fruit and carry them out of the field.
Water at the base, not over the plants, and drain the field well.
Keep insects that wound flowers and fruit down, and handle the plants gently.
Avoid planting so that flowering falls in the hottest, wettest weeks when you can.
diseases.threshold: In hot, wet weeks check flowers, young fruit and growing tips daily for a soft, wet rot topped with fine dark whiskers. Pick off and remove rotting parts at once. Sprays rarely pay.

diseases.name: Gummy stem blight
diseases.hint: Brown V shaped spots start at the leaf edge, and the stem near the base gets long brown lesions that crack and ooze gum.

sources.label: EWS Plant Doctor, Gummy stem blight
EWS Plant Doctor, Watermelon diseases and pests

melon: Gummy stem blight resists this group in many countries: use it only in turn with chlorothalonil or mancozeb.
cucumber: Gummy stem blight resists this group in many countries: use it only in turn with chlorothalonil or mancozeb.

prevent: Sow clean seed and plant healthy transplants. The fungus rides on seed and spreads from sick seedlings.
Rotate for at least two years away from all cucurbits, and plow under or remove old vines after harvest.
Water at the base or by drip, and keep the vines off wet soil with mulch or a trellis.
Avoid wounding the vines, and keep squash beetles down, since cankers start at wounds.
Space the plants and drain the field so the crown stays dry.
diseases.threshold: From the first runners, check the crown and the base of the vines twice a week for tan, water soaked cankers that ooze amber gum. Start protectant sprays at the first cankers or leaf spots in wet weather, and from the start where it struck last season.
diseases.rotate: Gummy stem blight has become resistant to the benomyl group (FRAC 1), the strobilurins (FRAC 11) and boscalid (FRAC 7) in several countries. Keep chlorothalonil or mancozeb as the base and turn the systemic groups.

diseases.name: Mosaic virus of tomato and pepper
diseases.sci: Tobacco mosaic virus and Tomato mosaic virus (tobamoviruses)
diseases.hint: Young leaves show light and dark green mottling, turn narrow and twisted, and the plant stays stunted.
diseases.no: No spray cures it. Pull sick plants, wash hands and tools, and never smoke while handling seedlings.

sources.label: DA RFO 02, Tomato Production Guide
ATI CAR, Tomato Production leaflet
EWS Plant Doctor, Tobacco and tomato mosaic

prevent: Buy clean, treated seed from a trusted seller, and plant a variety resistant to tomato mosaic where one is sold.
Wash hands with soap before handling seedlings, and do not smoke or chew tobacco while working with tomato or pepper.
Dip knives, pruning tools and stakes in diluted bleach or skim milk between plants and between rows.
Pull sick plants early, and work in healthy rows before sick ones.
Remove all old roots and plant debris after harvest, and rotate away from tomato, pepper and tobacco for a season.
diseases.threshold: Check seedlings before transplanting and the field every week. Pull plants with mottled, fern like or puckered leaves at once, and handle them last in the day.

diseases.name: Bacterial spot
diseases.sci: Xanthomonas spp. (Xanthomonas euvesicatoria, Xanthomonas perforans and relatives)
diseases.hint: Small water soaked spots on the leaves turn brown with dead centers, and fruits get raised, rough, scabby spots.

sources.label: EWS Plant Doctor, Bacterial spot
DA RFO 02, Tomato Production Guide

tomato: Copper only slows the spread, and many strains resist it: tank mix it with mancozeb to restore much of its effect.
chili: Copper only slows the spread, and many strains resist it: tank mix it with mancozeb to restore much of its effect.
bellpepper: Copper only slows the spread, and many strains resist it: tank mix it with mancozeb to restore much of its effect.

prevent: Sow clean seed. Soak doubtful tomato and pepper seed in hot water at 50 degrees Celsius for 25 minutes.
Plant only spot free seedlings, and raise them in clean trays away from older plantings.
Rotate for two years away from tomato, pepper and eggplant, and remove volunteers and crop debris.
Water at the base, not over the leaves, and stay out of the field while the plants are wet.
Plant a resistant variety where one is sold, and stake plants so leaves dry fast.
diseases.threshold: Check leaves and fruit every week, more often after storms. Start copper with mancozeb sprays at the first small, dark, greasy spots in wet weather. Dry season crops rarely need them.
diseases.rotate: Copper resistant strains of the bacteria are common in many countries, Asia included. Tank mix copper with mancozeb, and never use antibiotics on the field.

diseases.name: Gray mold
diseases.hint: Berries get soft brown spots, often under the green cap, that grow a gray dusty mold.

sources.label: UC IPM, Botrytis fruit rot of strawberry
Benguet State University, Disease management strategies in strawberry production in Benguet

strawberry: A protectant: spray from the first flowers in wet spells. It cannot stop rot already in the fruit.
Gray mold adapts fast to both parts: use it at most twice a season, in turn with captan.

avoid: Thiophanate methyl
Gray mold resists benomyl type fungicides almost everywhere. Thiophanate methyl rarely works on it.
prevent: Pick off dead leaves, spent flowers and rotten fruit and carry them out of the field.
Space and prune plants so air moves, and open the sides of tunnels on humid days.
Keep strawberry fruit off the soil with plastic or rice straw mulch.
Water at the base in the morning, and go easy on nitrogen, which makes soft, rot prone growth.
Pick often, handle the fruit gently, and cool it soon after picking.
bio: Bacillus based biofungicides and Trichoderma sprays on flowers lower gray mold under light to moderate pressure.
diseases.threshold: In cool, wet or foggy weeks check flowers and ripening fruit every two or three days. Protect from the first flowers in wet spells, and once grey fuzzy mold shows, clear the rotten fruit and spray at once.
diseases.rotate: Gray mold resists the benomyl group (FRAC 1) nearly everywhere and adapts fast to iprodione (FRAC 2), the strobilurins (FRAC 11) and the SDHIs (FRAC 7). Turn groups every spray and keep captan as the base.

diseases.name: Mosaic of tobacco (TMV and CMV)
diseases.sci: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV), Cucumber mosaic virus (CMV)
diseases.hint: Leaves show light and dark green patches, pucker and twist, and the plants grow slowly.
diseases.no: No spray cures them. TMV spreads on hands and tools, so wash hands with soap and do not smoke while working, and CMV comes with aphids. Pull out sick plants early.

sources.label: AGRIS, Pest clinic: a link among NTA researchers, extensionists and farmers

prevent: Plant a variety resistant to TMV where one is sold, and raise seedlings in clean, sterilized seedbeds.
Wash hands with soap before topping, suckering or transplanting, and keep cigarettes and chewing tobacco out of the field.
Pull sick plants early, and work in healthy rows before sick ones.
Keep tobacco away from cucurbit fields and weedy borders, where aphids pick up CMV.
Plow under old stalks and roots after harvest, and rotate with grains.
bio: Ladybirds, hoverfly larvae and small parasitic wasps hold aphids down. Avoid broad sprays that kill them.
diseases.threshold: Check the seedbed and the field every week, and pull mottled or distorted plants at once. Watch for winged aphids on young plants in the first month, the time CMV does the most harm.

diseases.name: Bacterial leaf spot of lettuce
diseases.sci: Xanthomonas hortorum pv. vitians (Xanthomonas campestris pv. vitians)
diseases.hint: Small water soaked spots turn angular and black between the veins, dry out papery, and heads can rot from the outer leaves.

sources.label: Nordis: new crop diseases found in Benguet (lettuce bacterial leaf spot)

prevent: Sow clean seed from a trusted seller. The bacterium travels in lettuce seed.
Water at the base or by furrow, not over the leaves, and do not work the beds while they are wet.
Rotate for at least a season away from lettuce, and plow under or remove old lettuce right after harvest.
Space the plants so leaves dry fast, and grow a tolerant variety where one is sold.
Pull and remove plants with many spots so rain does not splash the bacteria to their neighbors.
diseases.threshold: Check the outer leaves every week, more often after rain. Start copper sprays only when the first small, angular, black edged spots appear in a wet spell. In dry weather the disease stalls on its own.

diseases.name: Septoria late blight of celery
diseases.hint: Small yellow spots turn brown with tiny black dots inside and spread over leaves and stalks until the leaves dry up.

sources.label: Texas Plant Disease Handbook: celery
Pacific Pests, Pathogens and Weeds: Celery early blight

celery: Copper protects a little less well than chlorothalonil or mancozeb. Keep the leaves covered in wet weeks.

prevent: Sow clean seed. Seed stored for two years or more seldom carries the live fungus, or soak fresh seed in hot water before sowing.
Throw out any seedling with spots before transplanting.
Water at the base, not over the leaves, and space the rows so the plants dry fast.
Rotate for two to three years away from celery and parsley, and remove old celery leaves after harvest.
diseases.threshold: From transplanting, check the older leaves every week for small brown spots dotted with tiny black specks. Start protectant sprays at the first spots, and from transplanting in wet weather or in fields that had it before.

diseases.name: Strawberry leaf spot
diseases.hint: Small deep purple spots appear on the leaves, their centers turn gray to white, and many spots merge and kill the leaf.

sources.label: UC IPM, Common leaf spot of strawberry
Benguet State University, Disease management strategies in strawberry production in Benguet

strawberry: Use it at most twice a season and turn to another group between sprays, so the fungus does not adapt.
This group wears out fast on leaf spot fungi: no more than two sprays a season, in turn with another group.
This group wears out fast on leaf spot fungi: no more than two sprays a season, in turn with another group.
A biological: start before spots spread and repeat. It holds light leaf spot only.

prevent: Plant clean, healthy runners from a trusted nursery, and grow a tolerant variety where one suits your farm.
Cut off and remove old spotted leaves after the main harvest, so new leaves grow clean.
Mulch the beds and water by drip or at the base, so rain and water do not splash spores up.
Space the plants and do not overfeed with nitrogen.
Move beds to new ground every two or three years.
diseases.threshold: In the wet months check the young leaves every week for small purple spots that turn pale grey in the middle. Start sprays when spots show on many plants, before they join and dry the leaves.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.hint: Outer leaves brown along the edges and between the veins and collapse, while the inner leaves stay green and the plant stays small.
diseases.no: No spray cures it. Rotate with broccoli, plant clean runners of tolerant varieties, and avoid fields where it struck before.

sources.label: UC IPM, Verticillium wilt of strawberry
Benguet State University, Disease management strategies in strawberry production in Benguet

prevent: Plant clean runners of a tolerant variety from a trusted nursery.
Rotate with broccoli and plow its leftovers into the soil. Broccoli residue cuts the fungus in the soil.
Do not plant strawberry where potato, tomato, eggplant or pepper grew in the last few years.
Solarize the beds under clear plastic in the dry season before planting.
Pull wilted plants with their roots and destroy them away from the field, and keep weeds down.
diseases.threshold: Pull plants whose outer leaves wilt and dry first and cut the crown. Brown streaks inside confirm it. Remove sick plants at once. There is no spray threshold.

diseases.name: Stemphylium leaf blight
diseases.hint: Small pale yellow water soaked spots on the leaves grow into long tan to brown blotches that dry the leaves from the tips.

sources.label: East West Seed Plant Doctor: onion diseases and pests
Review: Stemphylium vesicarium, an onion pathogen, and options for suppression

onion: A protectant only and weak on Stemphylium: spray before the spots spread, and pair it with a triazole mix where one is registered.
garlic: A protectant only and weak on Stemphylium: spray before the spots spread, and pair it with a triazole mix where one is registered.

prevent: Plant healthy sets and seedlings, and throw out any with yellow streaked leaf tips.
Keep thrips and purple blotch down. The fungus moves fast into leaves already wounded or spotted.
Water by furrow or drip and in the morning, so the leaves do not stay wet through the night.
Rotate for at least three years with crops outside the onion family, and remove or bury old leaves after harvest.
Do not overfeed with nitrogen. Soft, lush leaves blight first.
diseases.threshold: In warm, humid weeks check the leaf tips and the side of the leaves facing the wind twice a week. Start protectant sprays at the first tan, water soaked streaks, and spray sooner in fields that had leaf blight the season before.
diseases.rotate: Stemphylium on onion has become resistant to the strobilurins (FRAC 11) and in places to iprodione (FRAC 2). Lean on triazole (FRAC 3) and SDHI (FRAC 7) mixes in turn with mancozeb or chlorothalonil.

diseases.name: Anthracnose twister of onion
diseases.sci: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides with Fusarium spp. (Gibberella moniliformis)
diseases.hint: Leaves twist and curl, the neck grows long and thin, pale sunken spots with tiny dark dots appear, and bulbs stay small or rot.

sources.label: DOST PCAARRD: UPLB work on onion anthracnose twister
DA Ilocos: help for onion farms hit by armyworm and anthracnose

onion: Turn it with propineb or iminoctadine and never spray it twice in a row, so the fungus does not adapt.
A strobilurin on its own wears out fast: use it in turn with propineb or a triazole mix, never twice in a row.
A biological: use it on seedbeds and early in the season. It holds light attacks only.

prevent: Use clean seed and raise seedlings in a clean seedbed. Never transplant twisted or spotted seedlings.
Time sowing and transplanting so the young crop misses the wettest weeks where you can.
Plant on raised, well drained beds, and water by furrow instead of over the leaves.
Rotate for two to three years away from onion, shallot and garlic, and remove leaf debris after harvest.
Feed with balanced nitrogen and potash, and keep weeds and thrips down.
bio: Treat the seedbed with Trichoderma mixed in compost, and use Bacillus based products early in the season.
diseases.threshold: From the seedbed on, check twice a week in wet weather for curled, twisted, yellowing leaves with sunken spots and orange spore masses. Pull twisted seedlings and plants at once, and start sprays at the first signs in the seedbed or the field.
diseases.rotate: Colletotrichum on onion can turn resistant to the strobilurins (FRAC 11) when they are sprayed alone. Use the triazole mix and turn it with propineb (FRAC M03) or iminoctadine (FRAC M07).

diseases.name: Yellow stripe and dwarf viruses of onion and garlic
diseases.sci: Onion yellow dwarf virus, leek yellow stripe virus, shallot yellow stripe virus and garlic latent viruses
diseases.hint: Leaves show yellow streaks or stripes, turn flat, crinkled and floppy, and plants and bulbs stay small.
diseases.no: No spray cures a virus. Plant clean cloves and sets, pull streaked plants early, and keep aphids down.

sources.label: East West Seed Plant Doctor: onion diseases and pests
FAO AGRIS: garlic transcriptome and the viruses threatening Philippine garlic

prevent: Plant clean, virus tested cloves and sets where you can get them, and renew your seed stock every few seasons.
Save planting cloves only from vigorous plants with no streaks, and grow them apart from the main crop.
Pull streaked plants early, before aphids carry the virus on.
Keep new plantings away from older onion, garlic and leek fields, and clear volunteers.
Use a border of corn and silver mulch to keep winged aphids off young plants.
bio: Ladybirds, hoverfly larvae and small parasitic wasps hold aphids down. Avoid broad sprays that kill them.
diseases.threshold: Check the planting every two weeks and pull dwarfed plants with yellow streaked or crinkled leaves, most of all in plots grown for seed cloves and sets. Spraying aphids does little against these viruses, so put the effort into clean planting stock.

diseases.name: Pineapple disease and butt rot
diseases.hint: Planting pieces turn red then black inside from the cut ends and smell like ripe pineapple, and the shoots die or stay stunted and yellow.

sources.label: Kerala Agricultural University, Sugarcane sett rot

sugarcane: Group 1 carries a high resistance risk: alternate the sett dip with a group 3 product where one is labeled.
pineapple: Dip crowns, slips or cut butts within a few hours of cutting. It protects, it does not save rotted pieces.
A dip for fruit butts after harvest and for planting material. Treat within a few hours of cutting.
Group 1 carries a high resistance risk: alternate the sett dip with a group 3 product where one is labeled.
A post harvest dip for fruit butts only.

prevent: Cut setts with three buds or more and plant them within a day. Long setts and quick planting cut the risk.
Plant in warm, well drained soil and not too deep, so the buds sprout fast.
Cure pineapple crowns and slips in the shade for some days before planting, so the cut ends dry.
Handle fruit gently, cut the stalk clean, cool the fruit quickly, and keep the packing area clean.
Disinfect cane knives and keep harvest bins clean.
bio: Trichoderma on setts and slips helped in some trials. Use it with, not instead of, a clean dip.
diseases.threshold: Two to three weeks after planting, check the gaps: setts or slips that rot red, then black, from the cut ends with a fruity smell show the disease. There is no cure in the field, so treat planting material whenever the soil is wet or cool and sprouting will be slow, and treat fruit butts within a few hours of harvest.

diseases.name: Ganoderma basal stem rot
diseases.hint: Several unopened spear leaves pile up, the old fronds yellow and droop, and hard brown brackets grow on the lower trunk.
diseases.no: No fungicide saves a sick palm. Dig out and chop infected stumps and roots at replanting, and drain and feed the palms well.

sources.label: Pacific Pests and Pathogens, Oil palm basal stem rot

prevent: At replanting, dig out the old stumps and their root masses, chop them small and let them dry, instead of leaving them to rot in the rows.
Do not plant new palms where an infected palm or stump stood without clearing its roots first.
Heap soil around the base of a lightly infected palm. It keeps the palm standing and yielding longer.
Keep the field drained and the palms well fed, with enough potassium, so they hold out longer.
Clear trunk debris and dead palms quickly, since brackets on them shed spores.
bio: Trichoderma and mycorrhiza added in the nursery and planting hole help young palms resist. They do not cure a sick palm.
diseases.threshold: Every six months, walk every row and look for palms with several unopened spears, drooping yellow fronds or brackets at the trunk base. Mark each sick palm and its neighbors. Fell, dig out and destroy palms that have brackets or have fallen.

diseases.name: Sugarcane smut
diseases.hint: A long black whip covered in a thin silvery skin grows out of the top of the stalk and sheds black powder.
diseases.no: No spray cures it. Plant resistant varieties and clean, hot water treated setts, and bag and burn the whips before they shed spores.

sources.label: JIRCAS, Selected Economically Important Diseases of Some Major Crops in the Philippines

prevent: Plant resistant varieties: they are the main defense.
Take setts only from a clean nursery, treated in hot water at about 50 to 52 degrees.
Pull out smutted stools, after slipping a bag over each whip so the spores stay in, and burn them.
Plow out badly infected fields instead of keeping the ratoon, and rest the land or rotate before replanting cane.
Do not bring setts from areas with smut.
diseases.threshold: Walk the field every two weeks from about two months after planting and count stools with whips. Bag and burn every whip before it sheds. The usual rule is not to ratoon a field where more than about 1 stool in 10 carries whips, but to plow it out.

diseases.name: Leaf scald of sugarcane
